2312.15874.problem: Establishing super-polynomial size lower bounds for a sum of ordered set-multilinear algebraic branching programs computing an explicit polynomial.
2312.15874.methods: Analyzing the dimension of the partial derivatives of the target polynomial under varying variable orderings to bound the capacity of sums of read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs.
2312.15874.regime: The setting of low-degree multivariate polynomials, specifically where the degree is bounded by the fourth root of the number of variables.
2312.15874.hypothesized_generalization: Proving super-polynomial lower bounds against general algebraic branching programs, thereby resolving Valiant's conjecture on the complexity of the permanent.

2103.09508.problem: The paper aims to establish the infinitude of a specific class of infinite Galois groups by analyzing the depth of their defining relations within a filtration.
2103.09508.methods: The authors analyze the filtration depth of group relations and the algebraic structure of unit groups in number fields to determine the size of the associated Galois groups.
2103.09508.regime: The results apply to the asymptotic behavior of class tower groups under constraints on the number of ramified primes.
2103.09508.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques suggest that a known theoretical upper bound on the deficiency of these groups is generically tight for most algebraic structures of this type.

1904.07062.problem: The paper addresses the problem of determining whether a given algebraic number field can be embedded into an infinite tower of unramified Galois extensions of prime power degree.
1904.07062.methods: The authors analyze the growth of class groups and apply Golod-Shafarevich-type criteria to the Galois groups of maximal unramified p-extensions of number fields.
1904.07062.regime: The results apply to algebraic number fields whose discriminants are divisible by a small number of distinct prime factors, specifically focusing on prime power discriminants.
1904.07062.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest a broader classification of number fields with infinite class field towers based on the arithmetic properties of their discriminants and the structure of their idele class groups.

2002.00502.problem: The paper establishes lower bounds on the number of distinct and unit distances determined by a finite set of points in a multi-dimensional Euclidean space.
2002.00502.methods: The authors introduce a deterministic, scale-dependent coordinate-inversion map called a compression, using its mass and gap statistics to translate coordinate-wise constraints into distance counts via elementary combinatorial summation.
2002.00502.regime: The results apply to arbitrary finite point configurations in Euclidean spaces of any fixed dimension, particularly in the asymptotic limit as the number of points grows to infinity.
2002.00502.hypothesized_generalization: The authors suggest that the compression framework and its associated gap statistics can be adapted to solve other extremal problems in discrete geometry and potentially interface with incidence-geometric and algebraic partitioning methods.

2312.17223.problem: This paper investigates the theoretical consequences of applying multicalibration—a strong group-fairness predictor guarantee—to classical complexity-theoretic equivalence and decomposition theorems.
2312.17223.methods: The authors construct low-complexity multicalibrated partitions of a domain to prove generalized, multi-set versions of the Hardcore Lemma, the Dense Model Theorem, and pseudoentropy characterizations.
2312.17223.regime: The results apply to arbitrary, potentially highly complex boolean functions and distributions over discrete domains, independent of any hardness assumptions.
2312.17223.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that many fundamental decomposition and regularity theorems in computer science can be systematically strengthened by replacing standard indistinguishability or multiaccuracy constraints with multicalibration.

2312.16653.problem: The paper addresses the problem of computing fair and stable utility allocations among cooperating agents in a graph-partitioning game where agents contribute vertices to a shared compatibility graph and the total utility is maximized via vertex-disjoint cycle packings.
2312.16653.methods: The authors introduce partitioned permutation games and analyze the computational complexity of lexicographical minimization and cooperative game theory solution concepts on directed graphs with unbounded cycle lengths.
2312.16653.regime: The results apply to large-scale collaborative networks with an arbitrary number of participating agents where the maximum allowed cycle length for resource exchange is unbounded.
2312.16653.hypothesized_generalization: The tractability of unbounded cycle formulations suggests that other NP-hard matching and packing problems on graphs can be solved efficiently under cooperative game theoretic frameworks if constraints on cycle or path lengths are relaxed.

2312.14916.problem: The paper analyzes the computational complexity of finding a local optimum under single-element reassignment heuristics for partitioning a set of points into clusters that optimize distance-based objective functions.
2312.14916.methods: The authors employ polynomial-time local search (PLS) reductions to map known hard local search problems to the Hartigan-Wong method for k-means clustering and the single-vertex flip heuristic for Euclidean Max Cut.
2312.14916.regime: The results establish worst-case PLS-completeness for low-dimensional Euclidean spaces, specifically for k-means with two clusters and Max Cut with squared Euclidean edge weights.
2312.14916.hypothesized_generalization: The hardness of these simple local search heuristics suggests that finding local optima for a wide class of geometric partitioning and clustering problems is fundamentally intractable in the worst case, even in low dimensions.

2312.17248.problem: The paper investigates the relative representation complexity and approximation error of different learning paradigms by analyzing the minimum computational resources required to represent their respective target functions.
2312.17248.methods: The authors construct specific Markov Decision Process families that encode NP-complete problems and evaluate the representation complexity of transition models, optimal policies, and optimal value functions using circuit complexity classes and multi-layer perceptrons with log-precision weights.
2312.17248.regime: The theoretical results apply to discrete-time decision processes analyzed under the asymptotic limits of constant-depth circuits and constant-layer neural networks with polynomial hidden dimensions.
2312.17248.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest a fundamental hierarchy of representation complexity in sequential decision-making where learning environmental dynamics is computationally easier than learning optimal behavior, which in turn is easier than learning the long-term expected utility of actions.

2312.15087.problem: Determining whether a weak, adversarially corrupted source of discrete random variables can be deterministically mapped to a shorter sequence with a higher concentration of entropy.
2312.15087.methods: Constructing probabilistic and explicit deterministic mapping functions using a novel class of seeded extractors that minimize output length, while proving impossibility bounds by analyzing the limits of adversarial manipulation on symbol-fixing distributions.
2312.15087.regime: Settings where a constant fraction of symbols in a sequence are uniformly random and the remaining symbols are adversarially corrupted, specifically focusing on the transition between two-thirds and one-half density of good symbols.
2312.15087.hypothesized_generalization: The existence of excellent condensers for SHELA and almost Chor-Goldreich sources suggests that restricting the computational or temporal power of an adversary allows for deterministic entropy concentration even when deterministic extraction is mathematically impossible.

2312.15488.problem: Standard asymptotic complexity notations are restricted to real-valued functions and cannot represent or analyze computational resource requirements that lie in the complex plane or imaginary domains.
2312.15488.methods: The authors introduce a new complex-valued asymptotic notation, Zeta, and define a transformation mapping to project real-valued complexity bounds onto the Argand plane.
2312.15488.regime: The theoretical framework applies to asymptotic resource analysis of algorithms where computational costs are modeled using complex numbers.
2312.15488.hypothesized_generalization: The introduction of complex-valued asymptotic bounds suggests that multi-dimensional or non-Euclidean resource spaces can be formally analyzed using generalized geometric transformations of classical complexity classes.

1105.6164.problem: The paper addresses the problem of efficiently computing and tracking the transition probabilities of synthesized binary-input memoryless channels to identify the most reliable channels for error-correcting codes.
1105.6164.methods: The authors employ degrading and upgrading channel approximation algorithms that merge output alphabet symbols to bound the capacity of the synthesized channels from above and below.
1105.6164.regime: The results apply to any binary-input memoryless symmetric channel under successive cancellation decoding, scaling efficiently to large block lengths.
1105.6164.hypothesized_generalization: The approximation techniques using alphabet reduction could generalize to tracking state transitions in more complex multi-dimensional or non-binary belief propagation systems.

2312.16125.problem: The paper identifies and demonstrates a critical flaw in a previously proposed linear-time encoding algorithm for general Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes, proving that the algorithm fails to correctly encode the code defined by the input matrix.
2312.16125.methods: The authors construct a specific counterexample matrix and analyze its structural decomposition into submatrices, focusing on the properties of Encoding Stopping Sets (ESS) and Pseudo-Trees within bipartite graph representations of linear codes.
2312.16125.regime: The result applies to the theoretical complexity bounds of encoding general linear codes, specifically demonstrating the invalidity of a universal linear-time encoding claim for arbitrary LDPC parity-check matrices.
2312.16125.hypothesized_generalization: The failure of this decomposition method suggests that general LDPC codes cannot be encoded in linear time without structural restrictions, hinting that sub-quadratic encoding complexity may be fundamentally unachievable for arbitrary parity-check matrices.

2401.00454.problem: This paper characterizes the relationship between quantum and classical communication complexities, as well as the validity of the Log-rank and Log-approximate-rank Conjectures, for functions that are invariant under permutations of their inputs.
2401.00454.methods: The authors analyze the approximate rank and communication complexity measures of permutation-invariant Boolean functions to establish quadratic equivalence between randomized and quantum models.
2401.00454.regime: The results apply to total and non-trivial partial permutation-invariant Boolean functions in both randomized and quantum communication settings.
2401.00454.thought_generalization: The findings suggest that structural symmetry in a function's input space generally prevents exponential quantum speedups across different models of computation, including communication complexity.

2401.01302.problem: Given a tuple of matrices, the problem is to determine the existence, uniqueness, and efficient computation of a larger, block-structured commuting matrix tuple that extends the original tuple.
2401.01302.methods: The approach uses linear algebraic direct sum decompositions of matrix commutator subspaces to reconstruct the unknown block components by solving a sequence of linear systems.
2401.01302.regime: The results apply to tuples of three or more matrices of size $n$ over any field, specifically in the regime where the target extension size is $n+1$.
2401.01302.hypothesized_generalization: The constructive linear algebraic methods hint that the worst-case complexity of computing commuting extensions, which is currently of unknown hardness, might be solvable in polynomial time for broader classes of matrix completion problems.

2401.01633.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of establishing fundamental complexity-theoretic properties, such as collapse theorems, error reduction, and circuit lower bounds, for quantum-verifier-based generalizations of the polynomial-time hierarchy.
2401.01633.methods: The authors analyze alternating quantifiers over classical, mixed quantum, and pure quantum proofs using an asymmetric product test for quantum states and structural complexity reductions.
2401.01633.regime: The results apply to the asymptotic complexity of polynomial-time quantum computations with alternating existential and universal quantifiers of polynomial length.
2401.01633.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that classical structural complexity collapses and circuit lower bound theorems can be systematically generalized to quantum complexity classes by properly accounting for the tensor product structure of quantum proofs.

2401.03924.problem: The paper addresses the exact matching problem, which asks whether a given graph contains a perfect matching with a specified number of red edges.
2401.03924.methods: The authors utilize algebraic algorithms and randomized techniques operating on Tutte matrices and polynomial identity testing over finite fields.
2401.03924.regime: The results apply to dense graphs, specifically where the minimum degree of the graph is bounded from below by a fraction of the number of vertices.
2401.03924.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques suggest that the exact matching problem might be solvable in randomized polynomial time for broader classes of graphs with dense subgraphs or bounded clique-width.

2401.05321.problem: The paper establishes lower bounds on the trade-off between execution time and memory capacity for solving fundamental linear algebra problems, such as matrix-vector and matrix-matrix multiplication, on quantum architectures.
2401.05321.methods: The authors combine a quantum recording-query technique with a novel bucketing method and direct product theorems to bound the success probability of quantum circuits.
2401.05321.regime: The results apply to quantum query algorithms and quantum circuits with restricted memory capacity (qubits) operating on explicit, structured, or binary input matrices.
2401.05321.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that for fundamental data-processing and algebraic tasks where inputs are highly correlated, quantum architectures cannot bypass classical physical limits on the product of time and space complexity.

2401.00947.problem: This paper investigates the limits of deterministic, fixed-size algorithms in solving the Boolean satisfiability problem by analyzing the minimum information content required to map problem instances to their correct solutions.
2401.00947.methods: The authors employ information-theoretic complexity bounds and algorithmic information theory to analyze the scaling of the state-space mapping of string relations under both uniform and logarithmic cost criteria.
2401.00947.regime: The analysis applies to asymptotic instance sizes where the information content of the problem class exponentially exceeds the fixed bit-length of any deterministic, non-randomized algorithm's code.
2401.00947.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that NP-complete problems cannot be solved in polynomial time by deterministic algorithms of fixed description length because the information content of the solution space scales exponentially with the input size.

2401.03263.problem: The paper addresses the problem of minimizing the size of a tree representation that computes a set of multiple Boolean AND-functions with overlapping variable sets.
2401.03263.methods: The approach analyzes how the degree of overlap among variable sets affects the computational complexity of constructing optimal tree structures.
2401.03263.regime: The results apply to the theoretical analysis of multi-output Boolean function minimization, specifically characterizing the transition between tractable tree construction and cases where the optimal solution size becomes large.
2401.03263.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest a general threshold behavior in multi-output function optimization where the tractability of joint representation is determined by a critical density of shared variables.

2401.06512.problem: The problem is to find a unique strict saddlepoint in a matrix of comparable elements, which is an entry that is the strict maximum of its row and the strict minimum of its column, or to determine that no such entry exists.
2401.06512.methods: The method uses a randomized Las Vegas algorithm based on random sampling to identify horizontal and vertical pivot elements, which are then used to iteratively eliminate a constant fraction of candidate rows and columns.
2401.06512.regime: The result applies to the discrete, comparison-based complexity regime for arbitrary square and non-square matrices of size n-by-m, operating under a randomized model with high probability.
2401.06512.hypothesized_generalization: The optimal randomized linear-time complexity achieved here hints that a deterministic linear-time algorithm for finding a strict saddlepoint may also exist, bypassing the sorting-based lower bounds of previous deterministic approaches.

2401.01193.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of proving computational complexity lower bounds for decision problems where heuristic strategies can typically bypass exhaustive search.
2401.01193.methods: The authors employ a constructive white-box diagonalization method combined with the concept of algorithm designability to analyze constraint satisfaction problems with large domains and boolean satisfiability problems with long clauses.
2401.01193.regime: The analysis applies to asymptotic complexity limits of NP-complete problems, specifically focusing on the transition from structured instances to those with almost independent solution spaces.
2401.01193.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that establishing algorithmic impossibility for complex decision problems requires constructing concrete, hard instances to bypass traditional relativization and natural proof barriers.

2401.07549.problem: Characterize the computability and possible values of a conjugacy invariant that measures the growth rate of boundary-extension configurations in multidimensional symbolic systems.
2401.07549.methods: Analyze the complexity of extender sets and extender entropies using computability theory, specifically characterizing them in terms of right-computable real numbers and the arithmetical hierarchy.
2401.07549.regime: Multidimensional symbolic dynamical systems, specifically effective, sofic, and computable subshifts in dimensions two and higher.
2401.07549.hypothesized_generalization: The equivalence of possible extender entropy values between sofic and effective subshifts suggests that this topological invariant cannot be used to topologically separate these two classes of multidimensional systems.

2401.07636.problem: The paper addresses the problem of determining whether two rooted tree graphs are structurally identical, known as the rooted tree isomorphism problem.
2401.07636.methods: The approach utilizes a linear-time canonical labeling algorithm that recursively assigns unique identifiers to tree nodes based on the sorted multiset of their children's labels.
2401.07636.regime: The result applies to the deterministic, sequential processing of finite, unordered rooted trees of arbitrary size, achieving optimal linear time complexity.
2401.07636.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques hint at a generalization toward efficient canonical labeling and isomorphism testing for broader classes of graphs with bounded treewidth or similar hierarchical decompositions.

2401.07242.problem: The paper investigates the query complexity of determining whether a given subset of a vector space over a finite field can be represented as the sumset of some other subset, as well as the related problems of shift testing and certifying that a perturbed set is not a sumset.
2401.07242.methods: The authors analyze query complexity lower bounds and algorithmic guarantees using property testing frameworks, linear-algebraic tools, and smoothed analysis on subset membership oracles.
2401.07242.regime: The results apply to sublinear-time algorithms and property testing regimes over the vector space $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ where the dimension $n$ grows asymptotically large.
2401.07242.thought: The paper establishes fundamental hardness limits for sumset recognition in finite fields, hinting that property testing of algebraic structures defined by existential combinations of sets is generally intractable without structured query access.
2401.07242.hypothesized_generalization: The hardness results suggest that testing membership in the class of sumsets, and more broadly testing properties defined by existential set operations, requires query complexity that scales with the domain size rather than remaining constant.

2401.07914.problem: The paper aims to provide a complete, diagrammatic axiomatization for the category of symplectic relations, which represents linear canonical transformations in classical mechanics.
2401.07914.methods: The authors construct a graphical calculus based on generators and relations, utilizing the algebraic structure of interacting Hopf algebras and Frobenius algebras to represent Lagrangian subspaces.
2401.07914.regime: The results apply to finite-dimensional symplectic vector spaces over arbitrary fields, with particular relevance to linear physical systems and quantum-classical interfaces.
2401.07914.hypothesized_generalization: The diagrammatic framework hints at a unified categorical formulation for infinite-dimensional symplectic geometry and the quantization of non-linear classical systems.

2401.08445.problem: The lack of a unifying variety theorem and complete equational logic for algebraic structures whose operations are constrained by general, non-classical relational properties such as generalized metrics, partiality, or partial orders.
2401.08445.methods: We use category-theoretic liftings of set functors to model relational signatures, and introduce parameterized clustered equations to capture conditional algebraic properties over infinitary Horn theories.
2401.08445.regime: The results apply to algebraic structures over arbitrary relational categories axiomatized by Horn clauses, including quantitative, ordered, and partial algebras of any cardinality.
2401.08445.hypothesized_generalization: The equivalence between clustered equations and abstract categorical equations suggests that Birkhoff-style variety theorems for any structured computational domain can be systematically derived from the properties of its underlying functorial liftings.

2401.09053.problem: This paper characterizes the relative computational complexity of converting non-constructive topological objects, specifically open and closed sets, into explicit countable representations.
2401.09053.methods: The authors analyze computational equivalence classes of partial type-2 functionals under Kleene's S1-S9 computability schemes and lambda calculus with fixed-point operators.
2401.09053.regime: The results apply to discontinuous functions and subsets of real numbers within the framework of higher-order computability theory.
2401.09053.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest a broader classification of mathematical theorems based on the computational strength of the structure functionals required to represent their underlying topological domains.

2401.10725.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of integrating automated geometric reasoning, formal proof verification, and interactive visualization tools to make mathematical deduction more accessible, rigorous, and applicable to education and design.
2401.10725.methods: The contributors employ interactive theorem proving, constraint satisfaction solvers, symbolic computation, and dynamic geometry software to analyze geometric configurations and generate human-readable proofs.
2401.10725.regime: The research applies to both Euclidean and non-Euclidean geometries within academic, educational, and computer-aided design environments.
2401.10725.hypothesized_generalization: The integration of automated deduction with dynamic visualization tools suggests a future where complex mathematical proofs can be automatically generated, verified, and translated into intuitive, human-readable formats across diverse scientific domains.

2401.11274.problem: The paper characterizes the relationship between unambiguous query complexity and parity-query complexity for boolean functions.
2401.11274.methods: The authors analyze the polynomial degree and decision tree depth of boolean functions under parity-query transformations.
2401.11274.regime: The results apply to the asymptotic complexity of total boolean functions in the query complexity model.
2401.11274.hypothesized_generalization: The bounds suggest a tight equivalence between unambiguous computation and parity-based query models for all boolean functions.

2401.10781.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of formalizing and reasoning about temporal properties and equilibrium states in dynamic systems where transitions and constraints are governed by metric time intervals.
2401.10781.methods: The authors extend dynamic equilibrium logic by integrating metric temporal operators that operate on transition systems and state-space trajectories.
2401.10781.regime: The proposed theoretical framework applies to discrete-event and continuous-time systems requiring precise quantitative bounds on state transitions.
2401.10781.hypothesized_generalization: The formalism hints at a unified framework for synthesizing controllers and verifying safety properties in hybrid cyber-physical systems under non-monotonic reasoning constraints.

2401.11686.problem: Analyzing the long-term evolutionary dynamics and strategy selection of multi-strategy, multi-player interactions on structured networks.
2401.11686.methods: Analytical derivation of strategy fixation probabilities and evolutionary stability conditions on regular graphs under weak selection.
2401.11686.regime: Multiplayer games with arbitrary payoff structures played on regular graphs under the limit of weak selection.
2401.11686.hypothesized_generalization: The analytical framework may generalize to arbitrary heterogeneous networks and stronger selection intensities.

2401.09270.problem: The paper addresses the problem of performing verified global optimization and parametric regression over continuous domains within a constructive mathematical framework.
2401.09270.methods: The authors formalize convergence proofs and search algorithms using constructive univalent type theory, instantiating them on ternary signed-digit and functional encodings of real numbers.
2401.09270.regime: The results apply to the setting of exact real arithmetic and constructive analysis, specifically operating on compact interval objects.
2401.09270.hypothesized_generalization: The framework suggests that a wide class of analytical search and optimization problems can be systematically verified and compiled into correct-by-construction algorithms using constructive interval specifications.

2401.11590.problem: The paper seeks to bound the minimum size of a linearly dependent subset of equations in a sparse system of linear equations over the binary field, which is equivalent to finding the minimum size of an even cover in a uniform hypergraph.
2401.11590.methods: The authors employ a combinatorial analysis of a novel variant of Kikuchi graphs, which are structured edge-colored graphs associated with the hypergraph, to avoid the use of matrix concentration inequalities.
2401.11590.regime: The results apply to $k$-uniform hypergraphs on $n$ vertices with $m$ hyperedges, specifically addressing the extremal trade-off between $m$ and the minimum even cover length for both even and odd values of $k$.
2401.11590.hypothesized_generalization: The results support the hypothesis that random hypergraphs are approximately extremal for avoiding short even covers, suggesting a smooth interpolation of the extremal trade-off between the sparse and dense edge regimes.

2401.10154.problem: This paper reviews the scientific contributions of Martin Davis, focusing on the formalization of computability, the definition and construction of universal Turing machines, and the solvability of decision problems.
2401.10154.methods: The analysis traces the development of computability theory using partial recursive functions, algorithmic enumerations of Turing machines, and the algebraic properties of computably enumerable sets.
2401.10154.regime: The theoretical results apply to the discrete, infinite domain of natural numbers and the foundational limits of algorithmic computation.
2401.10154.hypothesized_generalization: The historical progression suggests that the abstract concept of a universal computing machine is a ubiquitous property of both physical devices and natural systems.

2401.09234.problem: Determining the satisfiability of a system of boolean constraints where each constraint contains a large, fixed number of variables.
2401.09234.methods: Counting the number of unsatisfiable variable assignments generated by overlapping constraints without using existential quantification, inference rules, or search.
2401.09234.regime: Randomly generated instances of boolean satisfiability where the number of variables per constraint is relatively dense compared to the total number of variables.
2401.09234.hypothesized_generalization: The complexity of constraint satisfaction problems may decrease rather than increase as the size of the constraints grows, provided the constraints are sufficiently dense.

2401.09543.problem: The paper solves the problem of finding a linear-sized kernel for the independent set reconfiguration problem under the token jumping rule on planar graphs.
2401.09543.methods: The approach uses graph coloring, Euler's formula, and topological properties of plane embeddings to bound the size of projection classes and identify redundant vertices that can be safely deleted.
2401.09543.regime: The result applies to the parameterized complexity regime, specifically for fixed-parameter tractable algorithms on planar graphs where the parameter is the size of the independent set.
2401.09543.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques hint that linear-sized kernels for token-reconfiguration problems might be achievable on broader classes of sparse graphs, such as graphs with bounded genus or excluded minors.

2401.10310.problem: It is mathematically unclear whether deep learning algorithms can be implemented in a transparent and trustworthy manner under different physical models of computation.
2401.10310.methods: We construct a mathematical framework to analyze algorithmic transparency and apply it to deep learning solvers for inverse problems using Turing machines and Blum-Shub-Smale machines as models of digital and analog computation.
2401.10310.regime: The analysis applies to the theoretical limits of computability and decidability for neural network architectures operating on infinite-dimensional or continuous mathematical spaces.
2401.10310.hypothesized_generalization: Analog computing paradigms may inherently support mathematically trustworthy and transparent implementations of complex inverse solvers where digital computing paradigms fundamentally fail.

2401.11752.problem: Extending category-theoretic structures and their identity principles to an enriched setting within a constructive, univalent foundation where identity and equivalence are identified.
2401.11752.methods: Formalizing univalent enriched categories and constructing an enriched Rezk completion using the Rocq proof assistant and the UniMath library.
2401.11752.regime: Constructive type theory and univalent foundations, specifically operating on categories enriched over a monoidal category.
2401.11752.hypothesized_generalization: The constructive development of enriched Rezk completions suggests that higher-dimensional category theory and other enriched structures can be systematically formalized in univalent foundations without relying on the axiom of choice.

2401.09366.problem: The lack of a unified framework and formal connections between different category-theoretic approaches to initial semantics makes it difficult to compare and modularly prove the correctness of syntax with binders.
2401.09366.methods: We construct a pushout of two category-theoretic frameworks and generalize both to the setting of monoidal categories, utilizing a heterogeneous substitution formalism to provide modular proofs.
2401.09366.regime: This work applies to the theoretical analysis of typed abstract syntax, variable binding, and substitution systems within monoidal categories.
2401.09366.hypothesized_generalization: The successful integration of these distinct frameworks suggests that a wide class of algebraic and monadic approaches to syntax can be unified under a single, generalized monoidal category-theoretic formulation.

2401.10553.problem: The difficulty of formally verifying higher-dimensional algebraic structures due to the combinatorial complexity and infinite-dimensional nature of their traditional multi-sorted representations.
2401.10553.methods: We formalize a single-sorted algebraic definition of cubical categories using a proof assistant to verify the equivalence of the single-set and multi-sorted formulations.
2401.10553.regime: This formalization applies to constructive, computer-checked proofs of infinite-dimensional category theory within the Coq proof assistant.
2401.10553.hypothesized_generalization: The single-set algebraic approach could be generalized to simplify the formalization of other complex higher-dimensional structures, such as globular or simplicial categories, in interactive theorem provers.

2401.11898.problem: The automated completion of partially specified logical statements and their corresponding formal proofs is difficult due to the vast search space of potential geometric configurations and relations.
2401.11898.methods: The approach translates geometric constraints into a system of algebraic or logical constraints, solving them using constraint satisfaction techniques to simultaneously instantiate missing hypotheses and construct valid proof steps.
2401.11898.regime: The method is evaluated on synthetic geometry theorems and constructive proofs of moderate complexity, typically processed within interactive theorem proving environments.
2401.11898.hypothesized_generalization: The constraint-based completion paradigm can be generalized to other axiomatic domains, such as abstract algebra or program synthesis, where incomplete specifications must be filled to satisfy global correctness properties.

2401.12010.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity and tractability boundaries of a zero-sum bilevel optimization problem where a leader and a follower sequentially select independent sets from partition matroids defined over a shared weighted ground set.
2401.12010.methods: The authors develop polynomial-time solution schemes using single-level dual reformulations, dynamic programming, and greedy selection algorithms operating on partition matroid structures.
2401.12010.regime: The results apply to exact, non-heuristic optimization settings where the complexity of the problem is analyzed as a function of the number of groups in the leader's and follower's partition matroids.
2401.12010.hypothesized_generalization: The tractability of certain partition matroid interdiction classes suggests that more general multi-agent resource allocation and Stackelberg pricing games with block-structured constraints may also admit polynomial-time dual reformulations.

2401.12385.problem: The paper aims to characterize the complexity class of basic feasible functionals of type 2 using a syntax-directed, static analysis framework.
2401.12385.methods: The authors employ higher-order term rewriting systems combined with polynomially bounded cost-size tuple interpretations to bound the computational complexity of functional programs.
2401.12385.regime: The analysis applies to type-2 functionals over infinite data structures within the framework of higher-order term rewriting.
2401.12385.hypothesized_generalization: The approach suggests that tuple-based cost-size interpretations can be generalized to characterize higher complexity classes of functionals at arbitrary types.

2401.12638.problem: The paper investigates the redundancy and logical independence of the axiomatic foundations defining adhesive-like category structures used for double-pushout rewriting.
2401.12638.methods: The authors analyze the structural relationships between pushouts, pullbacks, and stability properties under slice constructions within category theory.
2401.12638.regime: The analysis applies to abstract category-theoretic frameworks with specified classes of monomorphisms, independent of any specific concrete model or implementation scale.
2401.12638.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest a minimal, non-redundant axiomatic foundation for generalized adhesive categories that could simplify the verification of rewriting frameworks in broader mathematical contexts.

2401.12641.problem: This paper characterizes the minimal degree of discontinuity for multi-valued functions on represented spaces by relating sequential discontinuity to Weihrauch reducibility.
2401.12641.methods: The authors analyze multi-valued functions on convergent sequences using Wadge-style games, completions of represented spaces, and first-order parts of Weihrauch degrees.
2401.12641.regime: The results apply to computable analysis and topological complexity classifications of multi-valued functions on represented spaces.
2401.12641.hypothesized_generalization: The equivalence between sequential discontinuity and specific Weihrauch degrees suggests that topological discontinuity in represented spaces can be fully classified by first-order computational complexity.

2401.13597.problem: The lack of a proof-theoretic, base-extension semantic framework for modal logics that can match the standard model-theoretic relational semantics.
2401.13597.methods: Defining accessibility relations directly over sets of atomic rules (bases) to inductively evaluate the validity of modal formulas, analogously to Kripke structures.
2401.13597.regime: Classical propositional modal logics, specifically systems K, T, D, and S4, evaluated over countable sets of atomic rules.
2401.13597.hypothesized_generalization: A unified proof-theoretic semantic framework that can generalize to non-classical modal logics and more complex relational structures on bases.

2401.13382.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of establishing complete, cut-free, and computationally tractable proof systems for regular languages without relying on complex hypersequential structures.
2401.13382.methods: The authors construct a co-intuitionistic sequent calculus using cyclic proofs to model least fixed points, and extend it with game-theoretic techniques to handle greatest fixed points for omega-regular languages.
2401.13382.regular_languages: The results apply to the algebraic and proof-theoretic representation of regular and omega-regular languages, specifically within systems lacking multiplicative product structures.
2401.13382.hypothesized_generalization: The simplified metalogical treatment of cyclic proofs in the absence of general products suggests that other fixed-point logics might be axiomatized more tractably by decomposing standard algebraic operators into asymmetric, action-like operations.

2401.12604.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity and relative hardness of search problems guaranteed to have solutions by generalized pigeonhole principles and Ramsey's theorem.
2401.12604.methods: The authors construct black-box oracle separations and lower bounds to analyze the reducibility between different parameterized complexity classes.
2401.12604.regime: The results apply to the black-box (oracle) setting for sub-polynomial and constant parameter regimes of the generalized pigeonhole principle.
2401.12604.hypothesized_generalization: The separations suggest a robust hierarchy of average-case complexity classes within TFNP, hinting that extremal combinatorial principles of varying strengths cannot be reduced to one another even under polynomial scaling.

2401.14303.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity and decision boundaries associated with recognizing and parsing formal languages generated by even linear grammars.
2401.14303.methods: The analysis employs reductions from classical complexity theory and structural properties of non-deterministic automata to characterize the hardness of language membership and equivalence.
2401.14303.regime: The results apply to the theoretical complexity analysis of formal language classes, specifically focusing on the boundary between polynomial-time solvable and NP-hard decision problems.
2401.14303.hypothesized_generalization: The complexity classifications established for even linear languages may generalize to broader families of linear and context-free languages with symmetric structural constraints.

2401.14106.problem: The paper characterizes the class of maps that satisfy the epimorphism property in a higher-dimensional, non-abelian setting where equality types can have non-trivial higher structure.
2401.14106.methods: The authors use synthetic homotopy theory and constructive type theory to analyze the fiberwise properties of maps and the contractibility of their suspensions.
2401.14106.regime: The results are fully constructive and internal, applying generally to any Grothendieck infinity-topos without relying on classical logic, the axiom of choice, or site presentations.
2401.14106.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that the class of fiberwise acyclic maps forms the left class of an orthogonal factorization system (a modality) in homotopy type theory.

2401.14623.problem: The paper characterizes the structural properties and classification of communication protocols that require only constant communication cost.
2401.14623.methods: The authors analyze the algebraic and combinatorial structure of communication matrices using tools from partition regularity and property testing.
2401.14623.regime: The results apply to the regime of randomized and deterministic communication complexity where the input size grows arbitrarily large but the communication budget remains bounded by a constant.
2401.14623.hypothesized_generalization: The structural characterization hints at a general equivalence between low-cost communication protocols and the existence of low-rank or low-complexity approximations for the underlying relation matrices.

2401.14996.problem: The computational overhead of verifying correctness certificates for hard decision problems is often prohibitively high because conventional non-interactive certificates can be exponentially larger than the input instance.
2401.14996.methods: The paper introduces an algebraic framework that maps a sequence of logical formulas generated by a decision procedure to a sequence of polynomials over a finite field, reducing the verification of the decision procedure's execution to an interactive protocol.
2401.14996.regime: The result applies to the verification of unsatisfiability proofs in automated reasoning, specifically targeting algorithms that can be modeled as sequential formula transformations.
2401.14996.hypothesized_generalization: The compatibility framework suggests that any step-by-step symbolic elimination algorithm can be efficiently verified in polynomial time by mapping its intermediate states to homomorphic algebraic operations.

2401.14645.problem: How to efficiently construct a single predictor that minimizes expected loss over an entire family of continuous loss functions compared to the best hypothesis in a benchmark class, without suffering from exponential complexity in the output discretization.
2401.14645.methods: The authors introduce sufficient statistics for loss minimization based on the approximate rank of convex functions, bounding the approximate dimension of univariate convex Lipschitz functions and lifting loss outcome indistinguishability to continuous labels.
2401.14645.regime: The results apply to the regression setting with continuous labels, specifically targeting convex Lipschitz loss functions, low-degree polynomial losses, and generalized linear models under weak learnability assumptions.
2401.14645.hypothesized_generalization: The connection between the approximate rank of function families and sufficient statistics suggests that many complex multi-task decision problems can be reduced to learning a low-dimensional set of moments or statistics.

2401.14383.problem: The paper addresses the problem of certifying non-negativity and bounding the extrema of continuous functions sampled from Gaussian process priors.
2401.14383.methods: The authors employ sum-of-squares (SOS) semidefinite programming relaxations applied to the covariance kernels and sample paths of Gaussian processes.
2401.14383.regime: The analysis applies to the asymptotic regime of high-dimensional continuous optimization and non-parametric Bayesian inference under smooth covariance structures.
2401.14383.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that semidefinite programming hierarchies can provide computationally efficient, tight approximation guarantees for a broader class of stochastic processes beyond Gaussian measures.

2401.15037.problem: The paper investigates the group of symmetries of spheres within the framework of univalent foundations, specifically analyzing the structure of their autoequivalence spaces.
2401.15037.methods: The authors employ homotopy type theory and synthetic homotopy theory to characterize the identity types and loop spaces of higher-dimensional spheres.
2401.15037.regime: The results apply to constructive and univalent mathematical frameworks, specifically within computer-checked formal proofs of algebraic topology.
2401.15037.hypothesized_generalization: The characterization of sphere symmetries hints at a systematic way to formalize and compute higher homotopy groups of spheres entirely within type-theoretic proof assistants.

2401.15456.problem: The paper aims to establish tight upper bounds on the measure of product-free subsets and prove product-mixing properties within compact continuous algebraic structures.
2401.15456.methods: The authors introduce novel hypercontractive inequalities on non-Abelian Fourier spectra, utilizing representation theory, harmonic analysis, random matrix theory, and differential geometry on Lie groups.
2401.15456.regime: The results apply to high-dimensional, quasirandom compact connected Lie groups, specifically focusing on the special unitary group and other simply connected compact Lie groups.
2401.15456.hypothesized_generalization: The developed hypercontractive inequalities and spectral concentration techniques can be generalized to establish new separation results in classical versus quantum communication complexity and broader geometric inequalities.

2401.15352.problem: The paper investigates the exact relationship between different complexity measures and the query complexity of composed functions, specifically focusing on whether perfect composition theorems hold for total functions.
2401.15352.methods: The authors analyze randomized decision trees, sabotage complexity, and distributional query complexity under product distributions, applying these techniques to the NAND tree function to establish polynomial separations.
2401.15352.regime: The results apply to the theoretical analysis of query complexity and decision tree models for total Boolean functions under randomized and distributional settings.
2401.15352.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that sabotage complexity and product-distribution query complexity can provide tighter, asymptotically larger lower bounds for randomized query complexity than linearized complexity measures.

2401.16296.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of transforming an arbitrary input graph into one that satisfies a target hereditary property by applying a bounded number of vertex splitting operations.
2401.16296.methods: The authors employ hardness reductions from classical NP-complete problems to analyze infinite families of forbidden subgraphs, alongside parameterized complexity analysis to establish tractability boundaries based on the maximum number of splits allowed per vertex.
2401.16296.regime: The results apply to the theoretical complexity analysis of graph modification problems, specifically distinguishing between NP-hard cases for properties like bipartite and perfect graphs, and XP-time solvable cases when the split budget per vertex is strictly bounded.
2401.16296.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest a general dichotomy where establishing hereditary properties via vertex splitting is intractable for most non-trivial graph classes unless the structural deformation permitted per individual vertex is highly restricted.

2401.16230.problem: The paper characterizes the subgraph-closed graph classes for which the first-order model checking problem can be solved in fixed-parameter tractable time with an elementary dependency on the formula size.
2401.16230.methods: The authors analyze structural graph theory properties, specifically characterizing the classes by the avoidance of certain shallow topological minors (trees of bounded depth and size) to establish elementary parameter dependencies.
2401.16230.regime: The results apply to sparse, subgraph-closed graph classes, generalizing settings of bounded degree and bounded pathwidth to those excluding a fixed tree as a topological minor.
2401.16230.hypothesized_generalization: The characterization suggests that elementary tractability of logical model checking is fundamentally tied to the exclusion of complex tree-like structures as shallow subdivisions within the input graph class.

2401.15186.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of finding approximate solutions to constraint satisfaction problems where the objective is to determine the boundary between tractable and NP-hard approximation regimes.
2401.15186.methods: The authors employ an algebraic framework based on fractional polymorphisms, generalizing them to plurimorphisms to analyze the structural properties of relational structures.
2401.15186.regime: The results apply to the classification of bounded-degree and promise constraint satisfaction problems over finite domains.
2401.15186.hypothesized_generalization: The algebraic classification of approximation complexity via plurimorphisms may extend to infinite-domain promise constraint satisfaction problems.

2401.15683.problem: The paper establishes lower bounds on the size and number of lines in small-depth propositional proofs for the Pigeon Hole Principle.
2401.15683.methods: The analysis employs random restrictions to simplify Boolean formulas of bounded alternation depth while preserving the underlying contradiction structure.
2401.15683.regime: The results apply to Frege proof systems of depth $d$ where $d$ is a constant or a slowly growing function of the input size, specifically analyzing the Pigeon Hole Principle with $N$ variables.
2401.15683.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques suggest that the gap between circuit complexity lower bounds and proof complexity lower bounds can be closed for arbitrary tautologies at higher depths.

2401.16336.problem: The formalization and computational verification of algebraic invariants and their multiplicative structures within a synthetic, homotopy-theoretic framework.
2401.16336.methods: Constructing group operations and ring structures on homotopy classes of maps into Eilenberg-MacLane spaces, implemented and verified using cubical type theory.
2401.16336.regime: Constructive type theory and computer-assisted proof assistants, specifically applied to finite-dimensional cell complexes and infinite-dimensional classifying spaces.
2401.16336.hypothesized_generalization: The computational techniques and simplified algebraic definitions developed here could extend to the formalization of more complex generalized cohomology theories and spectral sequences in synthetic homotopy theory.

2401.16366.problem: The paper investigates the computational power and descriptive complexity of decision problems that can be solved within polynomial space constraints without the aid of an arbitrary ordering on the input structure.
2401.16366.methods: The authors analyze the expressive power of choiceless polynomial time logic extended with spatial resource bounds, operating on relational structures and abstract state machines.
2401.16366.regime: The results apply to finite relational structures under resource-bounded computation where the input representation lacks a canonical ordering.
2401.16366.hypothesized_generalization: The characterization of choiceless polynomial space suggests a potential path toward separating complexity classes in descriptive complexity without relying on the assumption of ordered domains.

2401.16383.problem: The paper addresses the problem of learning logic programs from examples by identifying minimal unsatisfiable subprograms that represent contradictions between the current hypothesis and the background knowledge or constraints.
2401.16383.methods: The approach utilizes constraint satisfaction techniques and conflict-driven search to isolate minimal subsets of logical clauses that prevent a program from satisfying a set of positive and negative examples.
2401.16383.regime: The method is evaluated in the context of inductive logic programming and relational learning, where the search space of candidate programs is structured as a hypothesis space of first-order logic clauses.
2401.16383.hypothesized_generalization: The framework suggests that framing inductive synthesis as the iterative elimination of minimal unsatisfiable cores can generalize to other declarative synthesis domains beyond logic programming.

2401.17219.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity and algorithmic bounds for deciding the existence of a subgraph embedding from a fixed template into a dense host hypergraph under minimum or average degree constraints.
2401.17219.methods: The authors employ degree-stability properties, Zykov symmetrization, and reductions from the Exponential Time Hypothesis to analyze parameterized algorithms operating on dense uniform hypergraphs.
2401.17219.regime: The results apply to the asymptotic regime of large host graphs with a fixed template size, specifically focusing on dense instances where the minimum or average degree is a linear fraction of the vertex count.
2401.17219.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest a general threshold phenomenon where the computational complexity of subgraph isomorphism transitions from intractable to polynomial-time as the minimum degree of the host hypergraph surpasses a critical stability-based density threshold.

2401.17130.problem: The paper investigates the algebraic representation and characterization of block-ordered relations and their diagonal properties within relational calculi.
2401.17130.methods: The authors employ point-free relational algebra and order-theoretic properties to analyze the structure of binary relations and their decompositions.
2401.17130.regime: The results apply to abstract relational systems and discrete mathematical structures where order relations and block structures are defined.
2401.17130.hypothesized_generalization: The algebraic characterizations of block-ordered relations may generalize to more complex multi-valued algebraic structures and category-theoretic frameworks.

2401.17235.problem: Explicitly constructing infinite families of permutation codes under the Ulam metric that simultaneously achieve positive constant rate and relative distance arbitrarily close to one.
2401.17235.methods: Derandomizing a multi-stage shuffling process on hypercube-like structures by replacing random edge-swaps with structured choices derived from error-correcting codes over larger alphabets.
2401.17235.regime: Asymptotic regime where the permutation length approaches infinity, the relative distance approaches one, and the rate remains a positive constant depending on the target distance.
2401.17235.hypothesized_generalization: The generalized shuffling and derandomization framework may extend to constructing optimal codes under other non-canonical permutation metrics, such as the Cayley or Kendall tau distances.

2401.16998.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity and approximation limits of solving promise-valued constraint satisfaction problems by analyzing the power of linear programming relaxations.
2401.16998.methods: The authors analyze the Sherali-Adams linear programming hierarchy and generalize the Weisfeiler-Leman equivalence test from graphs to arbitrary relational structures.
2401.16998.regime: The results apply to the theoretical classification of promise constraint satisfaction problems under finite relational vocabularies.
2401.16998.hypothesized_generalization: The alignment of these hierarchies suggests a deeper, unified algebraic and logical framework for characterizing the limits of semidefinite and linear programming relaxations across all promise-valued constraint satisfaction problems.

2402.00791.problem: The paper establishes complexity-theoretic completeness and matching lower bounds for decision problems within high-complexity exponential-time complexity classes where such classifications were previously open.
2402.00791.methods: The authors employ Hausdorff reductions to map and analyze structural relationships between complexity classes within the exponential hierarchy.
2402.00791.regime: The results apply to the theoretical classification of computational problems within exponential-time complexity classes, specifically focusing on classes bounded by logarithmic query limits.
2402.00791.hypothesized_generalization: The structural properties of Hausdorff reductions may generalize to establish completeness results for other unresolved complexity classes within higher-order hierarchies.

2402.00331.problem: The paper aims to unify and generalize the notions of smoothness and properness of morphisms across different mathematical contexts by defining them abstractly in terms of adjoints to base change functors.
2402.00331.methods: The authors utilize the machinery of fibered and indexed category theory, specifically defining smooth and proper maps as those whose base change functors admit left or right adjoints satisfying Beck-Chevalley conditions.
2402.00331.regime: The results apply in the setting of general category theory and higher category theory (specifically infinity-categories) over a base category with finite limits.
2402.00331.hypothesized_generalization: The abstract framework hints at a unified, category-theoretic foundation for duality and pushforward operations that spans mathematical logic, topology, and algebraic geometry.

2401.17226.problem: Deciding equivalence and reachability properties for algebraic systems that violate standard syntactic reduction constraints, which previously required ad-hoc, case-by-case proofs of decidability.
2401.17226.methods: Defining a novel class of term rewrite systems based on graph-embedding and contracting relations, and proving their local stability and finite variant properties.
2401.17226.Regime: Infinite-state symbolic transition systems defined by convergent equational theories, specifically applied to cryptographic protocol analysis.
2401.17226.hypothesized_generalization: The structural properties of graph-minor and graph-embedding theory can be systematically mapped to term rewriting systems to identify broad, previously unrecognized classes of decidable equational theories.

2402.01011.problem: Determining the minimum number of rank-one terms required to represent a specific multidimensional array under algebraic symmetry constraints.
2402.01011.methods: Formulating the search for symmetric tensor decompositions over finite fields as a boolean satisfiability problem and solving it exhaustively using a SAT solver.
2402.01011.regime: Exact, non-asymptotic decompositions of small, fixed-size tensors over the field of integers modulo 2.
2402.01011.hypothesized_generalization: The non-existence of symmetric decompositions below a certain rank suggests that any potential improvements to matrix multiplication algorithms must break these specific structural symmetries.

2402.00502.problem: Axiomatizing language equivalence for nondeterministic finite automata generated by regular grammars using a minimal set of equations.
2402.00502.methods: Defining a process algebra with a recursion operator and proving a representability theorem up to isomorphism to map automata to algebraic terms.
2402.00502.regime: Finite-state automata and regular languages over a finite alphabet.
2402.00502.hypothesized_generalization: The algebraic axiomatization of language equivalence can be adapted to characterize finer behavioral equivalences, such as bisimulation, on the same class of automata.

2402.00962.problem: Unifying disparate notions of equivalence and simulation across deterministic, non-deterministic, and quantitative transition systems within a single, coherent categorical framework.
2402.00962.methods: Applying relation lifting and natural transformations to functors defining multiset transition systems, and utilizing categorical simulations based on preorder relations induced by epi-mono decompositions.
2402.00962.regime: Theoretical analysis of coalgebraic systems, specifically polynomial functors extended with a multiset constructor, applicable to alternating non-deterministic and probabilistic transition systems.
2402.00962.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that any quantitative or structured transition system can be systematically analyzed and compared by mapping it via natural transformations to a foundational multiset-based coalgebraic representation.

2402.01840.problem: The paper investigates the conditions under which iterated function applications on a structured set of logical formulas eventually stabilize into a periodic cycle, specifically analyzing this behavior in systems that lack local finiteness.
2402.01840.methods: The author analyzes the convergence of iterated substitution sequences on propositional formulas using algebraic logic, Kripke semantics, and formal verification in the Coq proof assistant.
2402.01840.regime: The results apply to non-classical propositional logics, specifically intuitionistic propositional calculus and its superintuitionistic extensions, which contain infinitely many non-equivalent formulas even within a single variable.
2402.01840.hypothesized_generalization: The existence of uniformly locally periodic sequences in intuitionistic logic suggests a broader connection between periodic sequence properties, uniform interpolation, and the definability of fixed points in non-classical modal and substructural logics.

2402.02602.problem: The lack of a formal, unified framework for reasoning about the computational properties and expressive power of high-level, abstract models of computation.
2402.02602.methods: Defining structural operational semantics and equivalence relations over abstract transition systems and algebraic process calculi.
2402.02602.regime: Theoretical analysis of abstract computational models independent of physical hardware constraints or specific programming language implementations.
2402.02602.hypothesized_generalization: A universal taxonomy of high-level computational models that classifies their expressiveness based on structural complexity and coordination mechanisms.

2402.02571.problem: The paper addresses the lack of standardized, reproducible test instances for evaluating and comparing algorithms designed to solve two-player zero-sum stochastic stopping games.
2402.02571.methods: The authors develop an instance generator and a benchmark library to evaluate the empirical performance of two distinct classes of game-theoretic algorithms.
2402.02571.regime: The evaluation applies to small-to-medium scale stochastic game instances designed to test computational complexity boundaries and algorithmic efficiency.
2402.02571.hypothesized_generalization: The benchmark suite will enable the identification of structural properties in stochastic games that dictate the relative performance of policy iteration versus value iteration algorithms.

2402.02567.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of transferring logical limit laws, specifically the first-order 0-1 and convergence laws, between different families of random relational structures.
2402.02567.methods: The authors develop a transfer tool that maps asymptotic logical properties and truth probability limits from unoriented hypergraphs to directed hypergraphs under arbitrary symmetry group actions.
2402.02567.regime: The results apply to finite random structures, specifically binomial random graphs and hypergraphs, in the asymptotic limit as the number of vertices approaches infinity.
2402.02567.hypothesized_generalization: The transfer tool hints at a general framework where logical limit laws of complex, highly structured random systems can be systematically derived from simpler, symmetric base structures.

2402.01078.problem: Constructing linear-sized hypergraphs that support a low-threshold agreement theorem, which guarantees that a collection of locally consistent functions can be approximated by a single global function.
2402.01078.methods: Constructing finite quotients of Bruhat-Tits buildings associated with the symplectic group to obtain bounded-degree high-dimensional expanders that lack small connected covers and exhibit swap cocycle expansion.
2402.01078.regime: The low-acceptance regime where the local agreement probability is arbitrarily small but positive, operating on infinite families of constant-degree, multi-dimensional simplicial complexes.
2402.01078.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that high-dimensional expanders derived from non-linear algebraic groups with the congruence subgroup property can systematically overcome topological obstructions like small covers to enable strong property testing theorems.

2402.01428.problem: Existing proof-theoretic frameworks struggle to natively integrate multiple distinct substructural logics and their structural properties without relying on complex embeddings or frequent modal translations that obscure proof-reduction behavior.
2402.01428.methods: The authors construct a natural deduction system for adjoint logic by defining a preorder over modes of truth to govern structural properties and establishing a Curry-Howard correspondence with an abstract machine.
2402.01428.regime: The framework applies to the design of type systems for functional programming languages, specifically where resource management, strictness, and monadic or comonadic effects must be verified statically.
2402.01428.hypothesized_generalization: The compatibility between preordered modes and structural properties suggests a unified categorical foundation for integrating arbitrary resource-conscious and modal logics into a single dependently typed programming language.

2402.03087.problem: This paper establishes the exact parameterized complexity of several fundamental graph problems, such as Scattered Set, All-or-Nothing Flow, and Dominating Set variants, when restricted to planar graphs and parameterized by outerplanarity, treewidth, and pathwidth.
2402.03087.methods: The authors employ parameterized complexity reductions to prove completeness for the complexity classes XNLP and XALP, operating on structural graph decompositions and planar grid-like structures.
2402.03087.regime: The results apply to the theoretical regime of parameterized complexity analysis on restricted graph classes, specifically planar graphs of bounded treewidth, pathwidth, or outerplanarity.

2402.02606.problem: The paper synthesizes and unifies algebraic representations, structural properties, and logical completeness results across non-classical logics, residuated lattices, and rough set theory.
2402.02606.methods: The authors employ twist-structure representations, Priestley-style duality, and algebraic isomorphisms to analyze and relate Nelson algebras, N-lattices, and rough sets induced by quasiorders.
2402.02606.regime: The results apply to the algebraic and order-theoretic structures of constructive and paraconsistent logics, specifically within the scope of finite and infinite Nelson algebras.
2402.02606.hypothesized_generalization: The equivalence between Nelson algebras and rough sets induced by quasiorders suggests a deeper, general correspondence between constructive logics with strong negation and information-approximation models in computer science.

2402.03069.problem: The paper investigates the conditions under which self-referential or recursive equations over discrete, algorithmic structures are guaranteed to possess stable, invariant solutions.
2402.03069.methods: The authors employ fixed-point constructions and diagonalizing operators acting on computable functions and their index sets.
2402.03069.regime: The results apply to the setting of infinite, discrete domains governed by effective calculability and Turing-equivalent models of computation.
2402.03069.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest a broader algebraic framework where fixed-point properties can be generalized to non-constructive domains and higher-order type theories.

2402.02829.problem: The paper investigates the expressive power of algorithmic procedures that extract intermediate logical invariants from proofs of implication, specifically determining whether these algorithms can generate all semantically valid invariants for a given implication.
2402.02829.methods: The authors analyze the completeness of standard invariant-generation algorithms by tracing the transformation of formulas and proofs within the sequent calculus and resolution refutation systems.
2402.02829.regime: The results apply to classical propositional logic, normal modal logics, and classical first-order logic, evaluating both cut-free proofs and proofs containing atomic cuts.
2402.02829.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that the incompleteness of invariant-extraction algorithms in first-order logic directly limits the constructive completeness of related definability theorems, such as Beth's definability theorem.

2402.01213.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of constructing models of mathematical theories that satisfy specific structural constraints on their interpretations, particularly when standard forcing techniques fail to preserve desired cardinalities or algebraic properties.
2402.01213.methods: The author employs forcing with language fragments and extends Namba forcing, operating on partially ordered sets of trees and formulas within infinitary logic.
2402.01213.regime: The results apply to the setting of set-theoretic forcing over models of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice, specifically focusing on the preservation of singular cardinals and the manipulation of interpretation constraints.
2402.01213.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques suggest a general framework for controlling the interpretation of first-order theories in generic extensions while preserving arbitrary cardinal structures.

2402.03134.problem: Constructing the patch locale and its universal property without relying on propositional resizing or impredicative assumptions.
2402.03134.methods: Constructing the frame of Scott continuous nuclei directly and applying a posetal instance of the Adjoint Functor Theorem to large, locally small frames with small bases.
2402.03134.regime: Constructive and predicative mathematics formalized within univalent type theory and the Agda proof assistant.
2402.03134.thought_generalization: The techniques suggest that other impredicative topological and locale-theoretic constructions can be systematically reformulated predicatively by utilizing large frames with small bases and posetal adjoint functors.

2402.01353.problem: Compiling rich, high-level logical specifications containing arbitrary user-defined variables and quantifiers into a restricted, low-level target language that only permits a fixed, finite set of variables representing external system inputs and outputs.
2402.01353.methods: Eliminating user-defined variables by solving simultaneous linear equations over high-dimensional tensor elements to express the specification constraints solely in terms of the system's input and output variables.
2402.01353.regime: Applicable to the formal verification of neural network properties, specifically scaling to high-dimensional input spaces like image tensors and complex multi-network specifications.
2402.01353.hypothesized_generalization: The variable elimination and constraint transformation techniques could generalize to compiling high-level specifications for other black-box or non-symbolic systems that restrict query interfaces to direct inputs and outputs.

2402.03273.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity and algorithmic boundaries of deciding the satisfiability of difference logic constraints, which restrict variables to pairwise differences bounded by constants.
2402.03273.methods: The authors employ structural parameterization and graph-theoretic decompositions, operating on constraint graphs to identify tractable fragments and boundary conditions of the decision problem.
2402.03273.regime: The results apply to the theoretical analysis of propositional and first-order difference logic formulas under various structural restrictions on the underlying constraint network.
2402.03273.hypothesized_generalization: The tractability frontiers identified for difference logic may generalize to broader classes of separation logic and linear arithmetic constraints over ordered domains.

2402.03274.problem: The paper aims to establish upper bounds on the number of variables required to uniquely define and distinguish graphs within a logical framework, specifically bounding the Weisfeiler-Leman dimension.
2402.03274.methods: The authors introduce the concept of Weisfeiler-Leman depth to analyze branching trees generated by recursive individualization and refinement procedures that partition graphs into independent components.
2402.03274.regime: The theoretical results apply to finite graphs, with bounds expressed in terms of structural parameters such as the vertex cover number.
2402.03274.hypothesized_generalization: The depth analysis of decomposition trees could generalize to provide tighter complexity bounds for isomorphism testing on broader classes of relational structures.

2402.03543.problem: The paper addresses the problem of establishing completeness and analyzing the computational complexity of decision problems for a quantitative propositional logic that can express polynomial inequalities over the non-negative real numbers.
2402.03543.methods: The authors employ the Krivine-Stengle Positivstellensatz from real algebraic geometry alongside a polynomial-time non-deterministic reduction to translate logical inferences into systems of polynomial inequalities.
2402.03543.regime: The results apply to finite theories within propositional logic, specifically analyzing the complexity of satisfiability and semantical consequence in both polynomial and affine settings.
2402.03543.hypothesized_generalization: The connection between logical completeness and real algebraic geometry hints that other quantitative logics can be systematically analyzed by mapping their proof systems to corresponding theorems of alternatives for polynomial or semi-algebraic systems.

2402.03685.problem: The paper determines the computational complexity of deciding whether one vertex configuration can be transformed into another via a sequence of adjacent swaps of distinct vertex types on a given graph.
2402.03685.methods: The authors construct a polynomial-time reduction from the non-deterministic constraint logic problem, building vertex and edge gadgets within the swap-relation graph to simulate logical AND and OR gates.
2402.03685.regime: The result applies to finite, simple, planar location graphs with a maximum degree of five, establishing that the reachability problem is PSPACE-complete.

2402.03891.problem: The automated complexity and runtime analysis of probabilistic programs is limited by the inability to prune infeasible execution paths and simplify control-flow loops.
2402.03891.methods: The approach integrates control-flow refinement natively into a modular complexity analysis framework, operating on probabilistic integer programs modeled as transition systems with non-deterministic branching.
2402.03891.regime: The technique is designed for automated static analysis of probabilistic integer programs, evaluated on a benchmark suite of loop-based programs.
2402.03891.hypothesized_generalization: Integrating path-refinement techniques with probabilistic transition systems suggests that non-probabilistic program transformation techniques can be systematically adapted to simplify the analysis of complex randomized algorithms.

2402.04134.problem: The paper establishes a lower bound on the computational complexity of multiplying two elements within a non-commutative polynomial ring.
2402.04134.methods: The approach utilizes algebraic complexity theory and bilinear complexity analysis applied to skew polynomial multiplication over finite fields or division algebras.
2402.04134.regime: The result applies to the asymptotic complexity regime where the degree of the polynomials approaches infinity.
2402.04134.hypothesized_generalization: The quasi-optimal lower bound suggests that multiplication in more general classes of non-commutative algebras might share the same fundamental algebraic complexity limits as commutative polynomial multiplication.

2402.04438.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of determining whether a given set of local constraints can tile an infinite grid without any violations.
2402.04438.methods: The authors analyze the structural properties of tilesets that are resilient to perturbations, using topological and dynamical properties of symbolic configurations.
2402.04438.regime: The result applies to the class of robust tilesets under standard two-dimensional grid configurations.
