2402.04438.hypothesized_generalization: The decidability of the domino problem may extend to other multidimensional symbolic dynamical systems that exhibit structural stability or robustness against local errors.

2402.04893.problem: Constructing a constructive and predicative model of extensional type theory within a minimal intensional type theory without relying on high-inductive types or non-standard axioms.
2402.04893.methods: Defining a cumulative hierarchy of iterative sets using W-types and showing it forms a category with families where decoding into h-sets commutes definitionally.
2402.04893.regime: Constructive and predicative univalent foundations formalized in Agda.
2402.04893.hypothesized_generalization: The construction suggests that other complex extensional type theories can be modeled constructively in minimal univalent type theories by utilizing structured trees to represent set-theoretic universes.

2402.04364.problem: The paper establishes a super-polynomial separation in size complexity between a restricted, read-once-like proof system and a more general, unrestricted proof system for establishing the unsatisfiability of certain propositional formulas.
2402.04364.methods: The authors construct a lifted stone formula using logarithmic-size inner-product gadgets and analyze its complexity by exploiting low-discrepancy and stifling properties of the gadget.
2402.04364.regime: The result applies to the asymptotic complexity of propositional proofs, specifically demonstrating an exponential size blow-up for bottom-regular ResLin proofs compared to ordinary, non-regular resolution.
2402.04364.hypothesized_generalization: The separation suggests that structural restrictions on linear queries in proof systems severely limit their efficiency, implying that general ResLin is fundamentally more powerful than its regular variants.

2402.05328.problem: The paper provides simplified proofs for the equivalence and properties of algorithmic complexity measures defined over quantum states, specifically addressing the behavior of universal quantum Turing machines.
2402.05328.methods: The proofs utilize trace distance and fidelity metrics to analyze the approximation of indeterminate-length quantum states generated by computable unitary operators on Hilbert spaces.
2402.05328.regime: The results apply to finite-dimensional and separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces representing quantum states of indeterminate length under universal quantum computation.
2402.05328.hypothesized_generalization: The simplified proofs suggest that algorithmic information theory can be consistently extended to continuous quantum systems and infinite-dimensional state spaces without losing the core invariance properties of classical Kolmogorov complexity.

2402.06294.problem: The paper analyzes how partitioning the components of a discrete dynamical system into blocks and updating those blocks sequentially affects the computational complexity of predicting the system's long-term behavior.
2402.06294.methods: The authors analyze the reachability and cycle detection problems of Boolean automata networks by mapping their update schedules to algebraic structures and transition graphs.
2402.06294.regime: The results apply to finite-state Boolean networks operating under block-parallel update schedules, ranging from fully parallel to fully sequential regimes.
2402.06294.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that the computational complexity of predicting network trajectories is fundamentally constrained by the interaction structure between update blocks rather than the local update rules themselves.

2402.04916.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of efficiently distinguishing non-isomorphic graphs that share identical global parameters, specifically focusing on strongly regular graphs which are notoriously difficult to classify.
2402.04916.methods: The authors construct simple, computationally inexpensive vertex and edge invariants derived from local subgraph counts and neighborhood intersection patterns.
2402.04916.regime: The proposed invariants are evaluated empirically on standard benchmark datasets of strongly regular graphs of moderate size.
2402.04916.hypothesized_generalization: The success of these simple local invariants suggests that polynomial-time graph isomorphism testing might be achievable for broader, historically challenging classes of highly symmetric graphs without resorting to high-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman refinements.

2402.04931.problem: The paper characterizes the computational complexity of finding a minimum-cardinality set of vertices whose deletion from a graph results in a cluster graph (a disjoint union of cliques) or a connected cluster graph, specifically when the input graph excludes a fixed induced subgraph.
2402.04931.methods: The authors employ graph-theoretic reductions, structural characterizations of forbidden induced subgraphs, and algorithmic design for bounded-treewidth or restricted graph classes to establish a complexity dichotomy.
2402.04931.regime: The results apply to the theoretical complexity classification (polynomial-time solvability versus NP-completeness) of graph modification problems on infinite families of graphs characterized by a single forbidden induced subgraph.
2402.04931.hypothesized_generalization: The dichotomy techniques suggest a general framework for classifying the complexity of other subgraph-deletion problems, such as block-graph or interval-graph vertex deletion, on H-free graphs.

2402.06740.problem: The paper investigates the minimum size of a set of reference vectors required to represent arbitrary Boolean functions under nearest neighbor and k-nearest neighbor decision rules.
2402.06740.methods: The authors establish equivalence relations between nearest neighbor representation complexity and Boolean circuit complexity classes, specifically analyzing min-plus polynomial threshold functions and depth-two threshold circuits.
2402.06740.regime: The results apply to asymptotic complexity bounds (both polynomial upper bounds and exponential lower bounds) for n-variate Boolean functions as the number of variables grows to infinity.
2402.06740.hypothesized_generalization: The connection between nearest neighbor representations and threshold circuits suggests that geometric classification models share fundamental representational limits with classical bounded-depth circuit architectures.

2402.07230.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of characterizing the algebraic and structural properties of principal types in lambda calculus by mapping them to specific classes of mathematical functions.
2402.07230.methods: The authors represent type structures and their unification processes as partial involutions acting on infinite discrete domains.
2402.07230.regime: The analysis applies to the theoretical foundations of type systems, specifically within the framework of intersection types and the semantics of system behavior.
2402.07230.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest a deeper, systematic connection between type inference algorithms and the geometry of interaction in linear logic.

2402.06397.problem: The paper addresses the problem of automatically finding gadget configurations to construct NP-hardness reductions for completion problems on pattern-avoiding sign mappings.
2402.06397.methods: The authors use a SAT solver to search and prune the space of partial configurations, combined with a combination lemma to assemble the discovered gadgets into complete hardness reductions.
2402.06397.regime: The method is applied to classify the complexity of thousands of non-isomorphic sign mapping structures of rank 3 and 4, as well as an infinite family of higher-dimensional structures.
2402.06397.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that automated search frameworks using CDCL-like pruning can systematically resolve the computational complexity of completion problems across a wide variety of constrained combinatorial and geometric structures.

2402.06821.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of deciding whether a relational structure maps to a target structure versus not mapping to a relaxed target structure, under structural constraints on the domain of the mapping.
2402.06821.methods: The authors analyze homomorphism-preserving maps and structural properties of relational structures, specifically generalizing tree-width bounds to a promise-satisfaction framework.
2402.06821.regime: The results apply to classes of relational structures of bounded arity under standard complexity-theoretic assumptions such as the parameterized hardness of the clique problem.
2402.06821.hypothesized_generalization: The sufficient condition for hardness suggests a complete classification dichotomy for promise constraint satisfaction problems restricted on the left-hand side, analogous to the non-promise setting.

2402.06803.problem: The paper introduces a novel class of graphs defined by a bounded average degree constraint on all induced subgraphs, and analyzes its structural properties, computational complexity of recognition, and the hardness of graph coloring within this class.
2402.06803.methods: The authors employ structural graph theory, recursive construction algorithms, algebraic monoid properties under binary operations, and polynomial-time reduction techniques to analyze the properties and complexity of these density-bounded graphs.
2402.06803.regime: The results apply to finite, undirected, simple graphs, particularly focusing on the computational complexity of decision problems like 3-coloring and class membership.
2402.06803.hyporhesized_generalization: The findings suggest that restricting graph classes based on uniform local-to-global density bounds can preserve NP-hardness for coloring problems while offering tractable structural decompositions and algebraic closure properties.

2402.07331.problem: This paper investigates the computational complexity of NP-hard graph problems when parameterized by the size of a hub—a small set of vertices whose removal leaves only small, disconnected components—to determine if the hardness of bounded-treewidth graphs is preserved under this simpler structural restriction.
2402.07331.methods: The authors construct parameterized reductions from the Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis, the Set Cover Conjecture, and the Max 3-Sat Hypothesis to various graph problems on structures consisting of a central vertex hub connected to constant-sized components.
2402.07331.regime: The results apply to the theoretical complexity analysis of exact algorithms on graphs, specifically in the regime of fine-grained parameterized complexity where the parameter is the size of a vertex hub.
2402.07331.hypotheses_generalization: The findings suggest that the exponential complexity of many NP-hard problems on bounded-treewidth graphs is fundamentally driven by local interactions with a small set of highly connected vertices rather than the global tree-like structure of the graph.

2402.07336.problem: The paper investigates how to formally represent and reason about normative concepts like obligation and permission within a broad class of non-classical logics that satisfy the selfextensionality property.
2402.07336.methods: The authors apply algebraic semantics and abstract algebraic logic to characterize modal-like deontic operators acting on the algebraic structures associated with selfextensional logics.
2402.07336.regime: The results apply to propositional, non-classical, and selfextensional logical systems that possess a well-defined algebraic counterpart.
2402.07336.hypothesized_generalization: The framework suggests that many standard results in classical deontic logic can be systematically generalized to any logical system whose equivalence relation is a congruence.

2402.07683.problem: This paper addresses the computational complexity of solving multi-choice search problems by establishing whether problems with arbitrary finite choice sets can be efficiently reduced to their binary-choice counterparts.
2402.07683.methods: The authors construct polynomial-time reductions between linear complementarity problems, unique sink orientations, and geometric ham-sandwich partitions by introducing an intermediate system of linear Bellman-type equations that utilize maximum and minimum operators.
2402.07683.regime: The results apply to the polynomial-time complexity class of total search problems (TFNP), specifically within the subclass of unique end-of-potential-line (UEOPL) problems.
2402.07683.hypotheses_generalization: The equivalence between binary and multi-choice formulations suggests that a broader class of multi-choice optimization and equilibrium problems can be structurally simplified to binary decision frameworks without loss of computational efficiency.

2402.08133.problem: The paper addresses the problem of distinguishing whether a given set of samples is drawn from a known reference distribution or from a truncated version of that distribution conditioned on an unknown subset belonging to a restricted family of low-degree polynomial threshold functions.
2402.08133.methods: The authors employ polynomial-time distinguishing algorithms and establish statistical lower bounds using moment-matching techniques and sample complexity analysis for degree-d polynomial threshold functions.
2402.08133.regime: The results apply in the asymptotic regime of high-dimensional product distributions, specifically contrasting polynomial-time algorithms using polynomial sample sizes against information-theoretic lower bounds requiring exponential sample sizes for constant degree thresholds.
2402.08133.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that computationally efficient truncation detection may be possible for a much broader class of non-convex truncation boundaries and non-Gaussian background distributions than previously established.

2402.08346.problem: The paper establishes tight upper and lower bounds on the computational complexity of two identification problems, Locating-Dominating Set and Test Cover, under parameterizations by treewidth and solution size.
2402.08346.methods: The authors employ Exponential Time Hypothesis-based conditional lower bound reductions and design matching dynamic programming schemes and kernelization algorithms on graphs and set systems.
2402.08346.regime: The results apply to fine-grained parameterized complexity analysis, specifically targeting tight single- and double-exponential time complexity and kernel size bounds.
2402.08346.hypotheses_generalization: The findings suggest that local, non-metric-based graph and set identification problems can systematically exhibit double-exponential complexity barriers under structural parameterizations, mirroring their metric-based counterparts.

2402.08434.problem: The paper classifies the computational complexity of solving systems of promise equations over monoids and groups, determining which instances are solvable in polynomial time versus those that are NP-hard.
2402.08434.methods: The authors employ the algebraic approach to promise constraint satisfaction problems, analyzing the homomorphic properties of monoidal minions and the richness of their associated polymorphism minions.
2402.08434.regime: The results apply to finite-domain promise constraint satisfaction problems, specifically systems of equations defined over algebraic structures like monoids, groups, and semigroups.
2402.08434.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that while a complexity dichotomy holds for promise equations over monoids and groups based on Abelianness, extending this classification to semigroups is as difficult as classifying all promise constraint satisfaction problems.

2402.08989.problem: Deciding whether two structures are indistinguishable under the family of homomorphism counts from a fixed, potentially infinite class of structures.
2402.08989.methods: Combining finite-dimensional representations of graph algebras with homomorphism tensors to construct a randomized polynomial-time decision procedure.
2402.08989.regime: The setting where the query class of structures has bounded treewidth and is recognizable under counting monadic second-order logic.
2402.08989.hypothesized_generalization: Homomorphism indistinguishability over a class of structures is decidable if and only if the class can be generated as a family of labeled structures using a bounded number of labels.

2402.08484.problem: The paper analyzes the computational difficulty of finding stable allocations and equilibrium prices in a discrete exchange economy where agents trade indivisible goods with personalized preferences.
2402.08484.methods: The authors employ complexity-theoretic reductions and algorithmic analysis to map the boundaries of tractability for matching mechanisms and price-clearing algorithms.
2402.08484.regime: The results apply to finite, discrete multi-agent markets with indivisible items under various structural restrictions on agent utility functions.
2402.08484.hypothesized_generalization: The hardness results suggest that finding stable market outcomes remains computationally intractable even under highly restricted preference domains, hinting at a fundamental limit to decentralized market clearing.

2402.09458.problem: The paper establishes the relative consistency of an axiomatic set theory containing matrix-like objects with standard Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory.
2402.09458.methods: The proof constructs a conservative definitional extension of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory using function symbols to define set matrices, followed by a syntactic translation and interpretation between the intermediate theories.
2402.09458.regime: This result applies to the foundational setting of axiomatic set theory and mathematical logic, specifically concerning theories with transfinite hierarchies and matrix-structured elements.
2402.09458.hypothesized_generalization: The relative consistency proof suggests that other algebraic or multi-dimensional structures can be consistently integrated directly into the foundational language of set theory without producing contradictions.

2402.09187.problem: The paper aims to classify the computational complexity of the quantified constraint satisfaction problem (QCSP) for temporal structures restricted to the Ord-Horn fragment.
2402.09187.methods: The authors analyze the complexity of quantified temporal constraints by establishing a complexity dichotomy (P versus coNP-hard) using algebraic and logical properties of relations definable over dense linear orders.
2402.09187.regime: The results apply to infinite-domain relational structures whose relations are first-order definable over the countable dense linear order without endpoints.
2402.09187.hypothesized_generalization: The dichotomy suggests a broader classification boundary for quantified constraint satisfaction problems over more general infinite-domain structures, particularly those defined by tractable fragments of temporal and interval algebras.

2402.09825.problem: The paper establishes tighter computational hardness limits for finding approximate solutions to parameterized optimization problems over lattices and linear codes.
2402.09825.methods: The authors employ gap-preserving reductions to map hard instances of parameterized problems onto nearest codeword, closest vector, and shortest vector problems.
2402.09825.regime: The results apply to the parameterized complexity regime under the Exponential Time Hypothesis, specifically targeting lower bounds of the form f(k)n^{\Omega(k^c)} for approximation algorithms.
2402.09825.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques suggest that many parameterized optimization problems on discrete algebraic structures share a common, optimal hardness threshold that cannot be bypassed unless the Exponential Time Hypothesis is false.

2402.09951.problem: The paper characterizes the conditions under which constraint satisfaction problems over infinite-domain structures can be solved by local consistency algorithms that guarantee a solution when no contradiction is found.
2402.09951.methods: The authors analyze algebraic properties of polymorphisms, specifically focusing on the existence of near-unanimity operations on homogeneous relational structures that exhibit finite duality.
2402.09951.regime: The results apply to infinite-domain constraint satisfaction problems where the template is a homogeneous structure with finite duality.
2402.09951.hypothesized_generalization: The characterization of strict width via near-unanimity polymorphisms might generalize to broader classes of infinite-domain structures that do not possess finite duality but share similar algebraic properties.

2402.09914.problem: The paper establishes the computational complexity of computing the Ekeland-Hofer-Zehnder (EHZ) capacity of a convex polytope, specifically showing that the decision version of this problem is NP-complete even when restricted to simplices.
2402.09914.methods: The authors construct a polynomial-time reduction from the feedback arc set problem in bipartite tournaments to the EHZ capacity computation of a simplex, mapping the optimization of a permutation matrix to the maximum acyclic subgraph problem on an auxiliary Eulerian directed graph.
2402.09914.regime: The result applies to high-dimensional convex polytopes (specifically simplices) with rational inputs, representing the asymptotic complexity class of the problem as the dimension of the state space grows.
2402.09914.hypothesized_generalization: The reduction technique suggests that other symplectic capacities or volume-related invariants of convex bodies may also be computationally intractable to compute exactly, even for simple combinatorial structures like simplices.

2402.10015.problem: The paper addresses the problem of bounding the worst-case running time of exact algorithms for NP-hard graph coloring problems.
2402.10015.methods: The authors employ a piecewise mathematical analysis that exploits varying structural properties of problem instances based on their parameter ratios.
2402.10015.regime: The results apply to the exact, exponential-time solving of NP-hard decision and counting problems on finite graphs.
2402.10015.hypothesized_generalization: The piecewise analysis technique can likely be generalized to improve the upper bounds of exact algorithms for other combinatorial optimization problems where instance difficulty is non-uniform.

2402.09971.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of calculating the vertex integrity of a graph, which is the minimum size of a vertex separator plus the size of the largest remaining connected component, when parameterized by various structural graph parameters.
2402.09971.methods: The authors employ parameterized complexity analysis, establishing W[1]-hardness via reductions from bin packing variants and designing fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms using structural decompositions like max-leaf number, vertex cover, and modular width.
2402.09971.regime: The results apply to exact, parameterized algorithms for NP-complete graph connectivity problems on structured graph classes where parameters like treedepth, feedback edge set, or modular width are bounded.
2402.09971.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest a sharp tractability boundary for graph vulnerability measures, hinting that single-exponential FPT algorithms for weighted connectivity metrics are achievable under dense structural parameters but become intractable under tree-like parameters.

2402.10293.problem: The paper addresses the loss of expressive power or computational efficiency that occurs when quantifier operations are restricted or eliminated in formal logic systems.
2402.10293.methods: The authors introduce a parallelized game-theoretic framework, termed 'parallel play', to analyze and preserve the structural properties of logical quantifiers.
2402.10293.regime: The results apply to the theoretical analysis of finite model theory and computational complexity classes, specifically within the domain of mathematical logic.
2402.10293.hypothesized_generalization: The parallel play framework may generalize to preserve expressiveness in other constrained computational models, such as restricted programming languages or limited-depth circuit classes.

2402.10360.problem: This paper investigates whether the sample complexity of learning an infinite hypothesis class can be fully determined by the sample complexities of its finite projections.
2402.10360.methods: The authors analyze transductive and PAC learning frameworks under proper and improper metric loss functions, employing a generalization of Hall's marriage theorem to establish compactness results for variable assignments.
2402.10360.regime: The results apply to supervised learning, agnostic learning, and distribution-family learning settings over both proper and arbitrary metric label spaces.
2402.10360.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that supervised learning under metric losses is fundamentally immune to undecidability pathologies, hinting that learnability is inherently a property of finite character for well-behaved loss spaces.

2402.10351.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of finding proofs in strong propositional proof systems when using quantum algorithms.
2402.10351.methods: The authors generalize the relationship between weak automatability and feasible interpolation to the quantum setting, reducing the hardness of proof search to the hardness of the Learning With Errors (LWE) problem.
2402.10351.regime: The result applies to the complexity class of quantum polynomial-time algorithms (BQP) under the assumption that lattice-based cryptography is secure against quantum adversaries.
2402.10351.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that quantum computers do not offer exponential speedups for automated theorem proving in strong proof systems, hinting that proof search is fundamentally hard even in the quantum regime.

2402.10174.problem: Verifying safety properties of systems whose state transitions involve non-linear integer arithmetic operations that are undecidable or computationally intractable for standard automated theorem provers.
2402.10174.methods: Constructing conservative linear overapproximations of non-linear constraints by mapping polynomial relations over integers to weaker linear integer arithmetic formulas.
2402.10174.regime: Static analysis and formal verification of smart contracts and discrete transition systems containing multiplication, exponentiation, or other non-linear operations.
2402.10174.hypothesized_generalization: The systematic relaxation of non-linear integer constraints into linear bounds can be generalized to automatically prove safety properties for a broader class of infinite-state transition systems without manual loop invariants.

2402.10494.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of formally verifying the existence and algorithmic computability of propositional quantifiers (uniform interpolants) within non-classical deductive systems.
2402.10494.methods: The authors construct constructive syntactic proofs using sequent calculi and formalize these proofs in the Coq proof assistant to extract verified functional programs that compute formulas.
2402.10494.regime: The results apply to propositional modal logics, specifically the classical systems K and GL, and the intuitionistic system iSL, operating on arbitrary formulas with countably many variables.

2402.11440.problem: The paper establishes the computational complexity of finding a sequence of moves that navigates a token to a target destination on a grid containing obstacles, where the token only stops moving when it collides with an obstacle or another token.
2402.11440.methods: The proof employs a polynomial-time reduction from a known PSPACE-complete problem to construct a gadget-based grid environment that simulates logical operations and state transitions.
2402.11440.regime: The result applies to the asymptotic worst-case complexity of the pathfinding problem as the grid size and the number of movable tokens grow arbitrarily large.
2402.11440.hypothesized_generalization: The reduction suggests that motion planning problems for multiple interacting entities on a discrete grid are generally PSPACE-complete even under highly restricted, deterministic movement rules.

2402.10783.problem: The paper addresses the problem of designing combinatorial selectors that can guarantee distinct, collision-free transmissions among a subset of active nodes in a network where communication channels are shared and uncoordinated.
2402.10783.methods: The authors construct and analyze permutation selectors, which are specialized families of permutations that guarantee bounded-size subsets of elements have distinct representatives under projection.
2402.10783.regime: The results apply to the theoretical, asymptotic regime of ad-hoc radio networks with a large number of total nodes where a small, unknown subset of size at most k is active.
2402.10783.hypothesized_generalization: The construction of these selectors hints that randomized coordination protocols in distributed networks can be systematically derandomized with only poly-logarithmic overhead using structured combinatorial designs.

2402.11531.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of determining the minimum dimension required for a combinatorial partitioning algorithm to uniquely identify a given relational structure up to isomorphism.
2402.11531.methods: The authors develop polynomial-time decision algorithms and establish complexity lower bounds using parameterized complexity analysis, group-theoretic properties of color class automorphisms, and logspace-uniform AC0-reductions on graphs with bounded color classes.
2402.11531.regime: The results apply to the theoretical and parameterized complexity analysis of finite relational structures, specifically graphs with bounded color classes and abelian automorphism groups.
2402.11531.hypothesized_generalization: The tractability of the identification problem for structures with bounded abelian color classes suggests that the boundary of polynomial-time solvability for isomorphism-testing algorithms is determined by the algebraic symmetry structure of the underlying color classes.

2402.11915.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of constructing optimal pseudorandom generators that can fool low-degree multivariate polynomials over finite fields.
2402.11915.methods: The approach utilizes algebraic and bias-reduction techniques operating on polynomial mappings and finite field structures to minimize seed length.
2402.11915.regime: The results apply to low-degree polynomials evaluated over moderately large finite fields where the field size is larger than the degree of the polynomials.
2402.11915.hypothesized_generalization: The optimal seed length achieved hints at the possibility of constructing near-perfect pseudorandom generators for broader classes of algebraic circuits and higher-degree representations.

2402.12169.problem: Automating the construction of fillers for specified boundaries within structured multi-dimensional interval frameworks, which is computationally difficult due to the complex algebraic constraints imposed by different interval transformation theories.
2402.12169.methods: The approach reformulates interval transformations as poset maps to solve boundary constraints, and applies constraint satisfaction programming to resolve Kan filling problems independently of the underlying interval theory.
2402.12169.regime: The method is implemented as an algorithmic solver evaluated on formal proof assistant benchmarks and algebraic topology verification tasks, such as the Eckmann-Hilton theorem.
2402.12169.hypothesized_generalization: The constraint-satisfaction formulation of boundary filling may generalize to arbitrary higher-dimensional rewriting systems and abstract homotopy type theories beyond cubical models.

2402.12068.problem: We characterize the computational complexity of finding pure, mixed, and symmetric equilibria in finite Bayesian games with discrete action and type spaces.
2402.12068.methods: We establish complexity bounds using polynomial-time reductions from circuit-satisfiability and Brouwer fixed-point problems, and construct a computational equivalence mapping between continuous and discrete game formulations.
2402.12068.regime: The results apply to multi-player games with discrete, potentially asymmetric belief distributions and discrete action spaces, with a polynomial-time algorithm specifically for symmetric settings under independent and identically distributed priors.
2402.12068.hypothesized_generalization: The computational equivalence framework suggests that complexity barriers and existence results can be systematically transferred between continuous and discrete representations of Bayesian games.

2402.13179.problem: Representing, manipulating, and verifying high-dimensional combinatorial structures with complex compositional constraints is computationally difficult and hard to visualize.
2402.13179.methods: The tool uses inductive cospan-based data structures, memoized recursive diagrams, and constraint-based geometric layout algorithms to perform typechecking, contraction, and expansion operations on globular cell complexes.
2402.13179.regime: The system is implemented in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly to run interactively within a standard web browser environment.
2402.13179.hypothesized_generalization: The successful implementation of this proof assistant supports the conjecture that every weak higher category is equivalent to a semistrict associative n-category.

2402.13716.problem: The problem is to find a set of mutually edge-disjoint paths connecting specified pairs of source and sink vertices in a directed graph where every vertex has equal in-degree and out-degree.
2402.13716.methods: The paper uses a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm based on a structural decomposition of Eulerian directed graphs.
2402.13716.regime: The result applies to directed graphs with Eulerian degree constraints, parameterized by the number of terminal pairs.
2402.13716.hypothesized_generalization: The structural analysis techniques may generalize to solve other routing and network flow problems on Eulerian digraphs that are typically intractable on general directed graphs.

2402.13086.problem: The paper aims to establish a unified structural connection between infinite tree representations, algebraic theories of operations, and the syntax of variable-binding calculi.
2402.13086.methods: The authors construct topological completions of algebraic structures using Lawvere theories and apply them to the syntactic representations of the lambda-calculus.
2402.13086.regime: The results apply to the theoretical setting of infinite-dimensional syntax, non-well-founded trees, and formal language semantics.
2402.13086.hypothesized_generalization: The approach hints at a general framework where profinite topological methods can systematically unify operational semantics and denotational semantics for arbitrary computational calculi.

2402.12875.problem: This paper addresses the theoretical gap in understanding how generating intermediate sequential steps computationally enhances the expressiveness of constant-depth, parallel-processing architectures.
2402.12875.methods: The authors analyze the computational complexity classes of decoder-only transformers with and without intermediate steps using circuit complexity theory and expressiveness bounds on constant-precision threshold circuits.
2402.12875.regime: The results apply to constant-depth transformers with constant-bit precision and logarithmic embedding dimensions operating on input sequences of length $n$.
2402.12875.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that auto-regressive generation allows parallel architectures to bypass depth limitations and simulate arbitrary serial computations of polynomial size.

2402.12514.problem: The paper aims to establish a precise algebraic characterization and equivalence for the formal structures used in contract-based system design, specifically by identifying assume-guarantee contract algebras with known classes of residuated lattices.
2402.12514.methods: The authors employ category theory and universal algebra to construct a categorical equivalence between the category of Boolean algebras and that of bounded 3-valued odd Sugihara monoids, subsequently mapping these to assume-guarantee contract algebras.
2402.12514.regime: The results apply to abstract algebraic structures of type (2,2,2,1,0,0,0) representing bounded distributive lattices with involution and commutative monoidal composition operations.
2402.12514.hypothesized_generalization: The equivalence suggests that other contract-based design frameworks can be unified and analyzed using the well-established machinery of relevance logics and residuated lattices.

2402.14751.problem: The paper determines the deterministic, randomized, and quantum communication complexities of finding a source, a king, and a maximum out-degree vertex in a tournament under arbitrary edge partitions.
2402.14751.methods: The authors employ reductions to the Clique vs. Independent Set problem, fooling-set arguments, and reductions from Set-Disjointness to analyze communication complexity, alongside decision tree rank and size analyses for query complexity.
2402.14751.regime: The results apply to finite tournaments of size $n$ under arbitrary partitions of the edge set between two communicating parties.
2402.14751.hypothesized_generalization: The equivalence between finding a source in a tournament and the Clique vs. Independent Set problem suggests that finding a tournament king can be viewed as a natural generalization of the Clique vs. Independent Set problem.

2402.14278.problem: Determining the minimum input dependency (locality) required for a vector-valued function to approximately sample from a uniform distribution over binary vectors constrained by a specific Hamming weight or modulo sum.
2402.14278.methods: Graph elimination techniques and local limit theorems applied to Boolean functions and product distributions over finite alphabets.
2402.14278.regime: Asymptotic settings with no restrictions on the input domain size, specifically analyzing the trade-off between locality and total variation distance.
2402.14278.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques suggest that sampling distributions with global algebraic or arithmetic constraints inherently requires superconstant locality, potentially extending to more general constraint satisfaction structures.

2402.13952.problem: The paper aims to prove the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which posits that any bounded, low-degree polynomial over the hypercube must have a coordinate with high influence.
2402.13952.methods: The authors analyze the structural properties of bounded low-degree polynomials under random restrictions, showing that with high probability they can be approximated by a small junta.
2402.13952.regime: The result applies to bounded, low-degree polynomials over the hypercube under random restrictions with a survival probability that is not too low.
2402.13952.hypotheses_generalization: The authors suggest that a full proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture could be achieved by showing that any potential counterexample can be modified (e.g., via composition or low noise) such that its random restrictions remain counterexamples, which would contradict their main result.

2402.15871.problem: The paper investigates whether a restricted, computationally simpler proof system can simulate a more general, unrestricted proof system under a relaxed notion of simulation that allows for polynomial-time formula transformations.
2402.15871.methods: The authors construct a regular resolution refutation from a general resolution refutation by introducing indexed copies of variables to track resolution depth, thereby preventing duplicate resolutions along any directed path in the proof graph.
2402.15871.regime: The result applies to propositional logic and proof complexity, specifically comparing the relative strengths of regular and general resolution proof systems for conjunctive normal form formulas.
2402.15871.hypothesized_generalization: The positive result suggests that other restricted proof systems separated under strict simulation might also be equivalent to their unrestricted counterparts under effective simulation.

2402.14932.problem: The paper characterizes the asymptotic behavior and stable limit sets of iterative applications of the Parikh mapping on formal languages.
2402.14932.methods: The authors analyze the fixed points and attractors of multi-dimensional vector sequences generated by applying Parikh vectors to language transitions.
2402.14932.regime: The results apply to infinite iterations of word-mapping operations over finite alphabets and context-free languages.
2402.14932.hypothesized_generalization: The stable attractors found in these language iterations may generalize to broader classes of non-linear dynamical systems operating on discrete symbolic spaces.

2402.14988.problem: Verifying the robustness of additive regression ensembles against bounded adversarial input perturbations is computationally intractable in the general case.
2402.14988.methods: The authors define a restricted class of tree ensembles characterized by a minimum feature-split distance and develop polynomial and pseudo-polynomial time verification algorithms operating on these structured decision boundaries.
2402.14988.regime: The approach is evaluated on tabular binary classification datasets using boosted tree models trained via a modified gradient boosting library.
2402.14988.hypothesized_generalization: Restricting the spatial density of decision boundaries in ensemble models can transition NP-hard verification problems into tractable complexity classes without severely degrading empirical predictive performance.

2402.15076.problem: The paper establishes the computational complexity of finding a sequence of valid state transitions between two configurations of a diffusion process on a graph such that the maximum size of the active set at any intermediate step is minimized.
2402.15076.methods: The authors employ a complexity-theoretic reduction from the label cover problem to construct a gap-preserving reduction for the target set reconfiguration problem.
2402.15076.regime: The results apply to the worst-case complexity of polynomial-time approximation algorithms on general directed graphs under standard complexity assumptions.
2402.15076.hypothesized_generalization: The tight inapproximability bounds suggest that similar PSPACE-complete reconfiguration problems governed by threshold-based activation rules will also exhibit strong inapproximability thresholds.

2402.17290.problem: This paper establishes complexity lower bounds for solving block-structured integer programs, specifically comparing the computational hardness of tree-fold and multi-stage integer linear programs.
2402.17290.methods: The authors employ complexity-theoretic reductions under the Exponential Time Hypothesis and prove unconditional lower bounds on the norms of Graver bases for block-structured constraint matrices.
2402.17290.regime: The results apply to the parameterized complexity analysis of integer programming, specifically in the asymptotic limit of the block dimensions and the number of hierarchical levels or stages.
2402.17290.hypothesized_generalization: The exponential gap in complexity between tree-fold and multi-stage structures suggests a fundamental asymmetry in hierarchical constraint propagation, hinting that transposing constraint matrices in structured integer programming inherently alters the parameterized complexity class of the problem.

2402.16777.problem: Estimating the relative frequency distribution of small, induced, connected sub-complexes within a larger hypergraph-like structure under computational constraints.
2402.16777.methods: Uniform sampling of sub-complexes to construct an empirical frequency vector, combined with a theoretical upper bound on the sample complexity required to guarantee approximation accuracy.
2402.16777.regime: Large-scale simplicial complexes with bounded sub-complex vertex sizes, evaluated on synthetic random simplicial complexes.
2402.16777.hypothesized_generalization: The uniform sampling and sample complexity bounds developed for simplicial complexes could generalize to estimating sub-structure distributions in other downward-closed hypergraph representations.

2402.15995.problem: Establishing lower bounds on the computational complexity of learning a target function composed of multiple linear threshold functions from high-dimensional data.
2402.15995.methods: Constructing a reduction from the parallel pancakes distribution to the intersection of halfspaces within the statistical query framework.
2402.15995.regime: High-dimensional settings where the number of halfspaces is super-constant and the statistical query accuracy is restricted to polynomial precision.
2402.15995.hypothesized_generalization: The parallel pancakes distribution may serve as a universal hard instance for proving statistical query lower bounds across a broader class of multi-dimensional geometric concept classes.

2402.17805.problem: The paper characterizes the exact computational power of graph neural networks when viewed as continuous models of computation operating directly on real-valued inputs and outputs, rather than restricting them to Boolean domains or logical classifiers.
2402.17805.methods: The authors establish a formal equivalence between graph neural networks and arithmetic circuits over the real numbers, mapping network operations to algebraic circuits that compute real-valued functions.
2402.17805.regime: The results apply to the non-uniform computational complexity setting for networks operating on arbitrary real-valued node features and graph structures of varying sizes.
2402.17805.hypothesized_generalization: The equivalence suggests that continuous-valued neural architectures can be systematically analyzed and classified using the established complexity classes of algebraic and arithmetic circuit theory.

2402.18193.problem: The paper addresses the problem of efficiently computing the number of discrete points contained within a parameterized geometric domain.
2402.18193.methods: The authors employ algebraic-geometric index theorems to relate the discrete point count to continuous topological invariants of the underlying space.
2402.18193.regime: The results apply to high-dimensional algebraic varieties defined over finite fields or complex numbers where direct enumeration is computationally intractable.
2402.18193.hypothesized_generalization: The approach suggests a general framework for translating discrete counting problems in combinatorial geometry into the computation of characteristic classes on associated moduli spaces.

2403.00390.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of equivalence, minimization, and weight synthesis for deterministic weighted automata whose outputs are only observable as membership in discrete intervals.
2403.00390.methods: The authors analyze state-merging algorithms, state-space minimization, and equivalence testing on deterministic finite automata equipped with interval-mapped weight functions.
2403.00390.regime: The results apply to formal language theory and active automata learning, specifically contrasting polynomial-time tractability under unary weight representations with NP-hard and exponential-weight bounds under binary representations.
2403.00390.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that active learning of quantitative systems under partial observability requires a more rigid equivalence relation than observational equivalence to prevent exponential blow-up in state and weight representation.

2403.01162.problem: Given a set of agents with heterogeneous preferences over a set of indivisible items, the problem is to find a one-to-one assignment and a corresponding vector of non-negative monetary compensations that minimizes the sum of compensations required to ensure no agent prefers another agent's assigned item and compensation bundle to their own.
2403.01162.methods: The paper uses computational complexity analysis, specifically a polynomial-time reduction to prove NP-hardness, alongside algorithmic design for special cases involving restricted utility structures and bounded parameter differences.
2403.01162.regime: The results apply to the discrete allocation of indivisible items to an equal number of agents under complete information, covering both general utility functions and restricted settings such as identical utilities.
2403.01162.hypothesized_generalization: The hardness result suggests that introducing continuous auxiliary variables to stabilize discrete assignment problems under inequality constraints generally leads to computational intractability, even when the uncompensated decision problem is solvable in polynomial time.

2403.00098.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of counting the number of zero terms in a sequence defined by a linear recurrence relation.
2403.00098.methods: The authors employ complexity-theoretic reductions from the Subset Sum Problem to analyze the counting complexity of zero sets of linear recurrence sequences whose characteristic roots are roots of unity.
2403.00098.regime: The results apply to arbitrary-order integer linear recurrence sequences, specifically focusing on the counting complexity of their zero sets within a bounded range.
2403.00098.hypothesized_generalization: The hardness results suggest that computing the exact size of the zero set for more general classes of exponential-polynomial equations is likely intractable, potentially extending to other decision and counting problems in dynamical systems.

2403.00115.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of determining whether an integer represented implicitly by a division-free straight-line program can be expressed as the sum of two or three integer squares.
2403.00115.methods: The authors analyze complexity classes and establish polynomial-time reductions between decision problems on straight-line programs, specifically connecting sign determination to sum-of-squares representation and polynomial degree computation.
2403.00115.regime: The results apply to the theoretical complexity analysis of constant-free, division-free arithmetic circuits representing exponentially large integers.
2403.00115.hypothesized_generalization: The connections established suggest that deciding algebraic properties of implicitly represented integers may share a fundamental complexity barrier with sign determination and numerical approximation.

2403.03530.problem: The paper characterizes the average-case deterministic query complexity of boolean functions under a uniform input distribution, specifically analyzing how this complexity scales with the function's weight (the size of its onset).
2403.03530.methods: The authors analyze the relationship between query complexity and weight by combining combinatorial bounds with Fourier analysis of boolean functions, specifically utilizing the Friedgut-Kalai-Naor (FKN) and Kindler-Safra (KS) theorems.
2403.03530.regime: The results apply to the class of all boolean functions with a fixed weight, ranging from sparse functions to almost all functions of a given weight asymptotically.
2403.03530.hypothesized_generalization: The tight bounds on average-case query complexity suggest that a function's structural complexity under random restrictions is fundamentally constrained by its low-level Fourier spectrum concentration.

2402.19365.problem: The paper addresses the problem of finding a minimum vertex cover on unweighted, simple, connected graphs, which is equivalent to determining the feasibility of a DiRe committee.
2402.19365.methods: The proposed approach combines maximum matching, breadth-first search tree level-tracking, maximal matching, and a local minimization technique to operate on unweighted undirected graphs.
2402.19365.regime: The result applies to the exact computation of minimum vertex covers on unweighted, simple, connected graphs in deterministic polynomial time.
2402.19365.hypothesized_generalization: The existence of an unconditional deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for this problem hints that certain classes of NP-complete graph problems might be solvable in polynomial time without relying on approximations.

2403.02275.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of proving lower bounds on the size of proofs required to refute random unsatisfiable formulas in bounded-depth propositional proof systems.
2403.02275.methods: The authors adapt deterministic restriction techniques to simplify bounded-depth circuits by fixing a small number of variables, combining this with expansion properties of random hypergraphs and resolution width analysis.
2403.02275.regime: The result applies to random 3-CNF formulas with a linear number of clauses, establishing super-linear lower bounds on the number of steps in bounded-depth Frege refutations.

2403.01965.problem: The paper addresses the problem of deterministically factoring multivariate polynomials that are represented by low-depth algebraic circuits.
2403.01965.methods: The authors introduce a pseudo-resultant operator to serve as a low-complexity proxy for the standard polynomial resultant, combining it with Newton iteration and identity testing algorithms.
2403.01965.regime: The results apply to multivariate polynomials of polynomial degree computed by constant-depth arithmetic circuits over rational numbers, operating in deterministic subexponential time.
2403.01965.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that the factors of polynomials computed by a restricted circuit class can themselves be efficiently computed within a closely related or slightly larger circuit class.

2403.02499.problem: Establishing a robust and physically meaningful definition of space complexity for continuous-time computational models governed by ordinary differential equations.
2403.02499.methods: Characterizing complexity classes algebraically by proving mutual simulations between Turing machines and continuous polynomial ordinary differential equations, and relating space complexity to the numerical precision required to solve these equations.
2403.02499.regime: Continuous-time dynamical systems simulating polynomial-space computations over both the integers and the real numbers.
2403.02499.thought_experiment_or_generalization: The equivalence between computational space complexity and numerical precision suggests that the physical limits of analog computation and deep learning models are fundamentally bounded by the noise and stability of their underlying physical substrates.

2403.03651.problem: The paper addresses the challenge of characterizing and constructing local codes whose local constraints can be consistently extended to global codewords, which is essential for ensuring strong global expansion properties from local structures.
2403.03651.methods: The authors introduce sheaf codes, which generalize Tanner codes using poset-based topological spaces, and define the property of maximal extendibility to analyze the propagation of local algebraic constraints to global sections.
2403.03651.regime: The results apply to asymptotic families of classical and quantum low-density parity-check codes, specifically focusing on multi-dimensional product codes and their coboundary expansion.
2403.03651.hypothesized_generalization: The authors suggest that defining sheaf codes on Ramanujan cubical complexes could provide a path toward proving the existence of asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes.

2403.03668.problem: The paper characterizes the structural properties of graphs that admit Hamiltonian paths and cycles when the size of the largest pairwise non-adjacent vertex subset is bounded by a small constant.
2403.03668.methods: The approach uses vertex connectivity thresholds and structural decomposition theorems to classify feasible graph instances based on their connectivity level and forbidden induced subgraphs.
2403.03668.regime: The results apply to the class of graphs with a small, fixed independence number, specifically focusing on the boundary where Hamiltonian problems transition from NP-complete to polynomial-time solvable.
2403.03668.hypothesized_generalization: The structural characterization of feasible instances for small independence numbers hints at a general classification theorem for Hamiltonian-type problems in graphs parameterized by their independence number.

2403.04694.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of finding a minimum dominating set under the constraint that every vertex outside the set has between one and two neighbors within the set.
2403.04694.methods: The authors employ dynamic programming on interval representations for the positive algorithmic result, and polynomial-time reductions on chord intersection models for the hardness proof.
2403.04694.regime: The results apply to finite, simple graphs, specifically establishing polynomial-time solvability on non-proper interval graphs and NP-completeness on circle graphs.

2403.09134.problem: The paper addresses the problem of enumerating all satisfying assignments of a boolean formula that lie at a specific Hamming distance from a given starting assignment, under the constraint that no satisfying assignments exist at a closer distance.
2403.09134.methods: The authors employ a randomized local search algorithm and analyze its expected running time using combinatorial bounds on monotone conjunctive normal forms and hypergraph Turán properties.
2403.09134.regime: The results apply to the non-trivial case of 3-CNF formulas with a Hamming distance parameter of 2, establishing bounds that scale exponentially with the number of variables.
2403.09134.hypothesized_generalization: The authors suggest that matching the theoretical upper bounds for this local enumeration problem would break the Super Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis and yield optimal, unrestricted depth-3 circuit lower bounds for the Majority function.

2403.10063.problem: The paper addresses the problem of online continuous adversarial DR-submodular optimization under various combinations of monotonicity, constraint set geometry, and feedback models.
2403.10063.methods: The authors propose projection-free Frank-Wolfe based algorithms that rely on solving linear optimization sub-routines over convex feasible regions.
2403.10063.regime: The results apply to sequential decision-making settings with full-information, semi-bandit, or bandit feedback under stochastic gradient or value queries.
2403.10063.hypothesized_generalization: The unified performance improvements suggest that projection-free Frank-Wolfe variants can systematically match or exceed the regret bounds of projection-based methods across a broad class of non-convex constrained optimization problems.

2403.04955.problem: The paper analyzes the computational complexity of determining the winning player in a disjunctive sum of independent, tractable combinatorial games.
2403.04955.methods: The authors employ complexity reductions to prove hardness on sums of superstars, which are a family of tepid, nearly symmetric games in canonical form.
2403.04955.regime: The result applies to the asymptotic complexity of deciding game outcomes under normal play conventions as the number of parallel game components grows.
2403.04955.thought_generalization: The hardness of these nearly symmetric, zero-temperature games suggests that even minimal asymmetric branching or parity-altering moves are sufficient to make parallel decision-making processes computationally intractable.

2403.11749.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of finding shortest non-separating simple closed curves on non-orientable surfaces, categorized by their topological properties such as sidedness and whether they orient the surface.
2403.11749.methods: The authors employ fixed-parameter tractability, NP-hardness reductions, canonical systems of loops adapted for non-orientable surfaces, and covering spaces constructed as quotients of homology covers.
2403.11749.regime: The results apply to combinatorial surfaces of size $n$ and genus $g$, distinguishing between NP-hard cases that are fixed-parameter tractable in $g$ and polynomial-time solvable cases.
2403.11749.hyporhesized_generalization: The techniques suggest that topological classification via covering spaces and homology quotients can be generalized to efficiently solve optimization problems for other complex, non-orientable surface structures.

2403.06248.problem: The paper establishes lower bounds on the randomized query complexity of finding a local minimum of a function defined over the vertices of an arbitrary connected graph.
2403.06248.methods: The authors employ a relational adversary method to bound query complexity using the mixing time and spectral properties of lazy, irreducible, and reversible Markov chains defined on the graph.
2403.06248.regime: The results apply to arbitrary connected undirected graphs under randomized query models, particularly where the graph's geometry deviates from standard hypercubes or grids.
2403.06248.hypothesized_generalization: The connection between query complexity and mixing times suggests that the hardness of local optimization on discrete structures is fundamentally governed by the spectral geometry and diffusion properties of the underlying search space.

2403.05074.problem: The worst-case time complexity of executing fundamental family algebra operations on binary decision diagrams and zero-suppressed binary decision diagrams remains unproven and disputed.
2403.05074.methods: The paper uses complexity analysis and worst-case input construction to analyze recursive algorithms operating on directed acyclic graph representations of set families.
2403.05074.regime: The analysis applies to the worst-case complexity of single operations on binary decision diagrams of arbitrary size.
2403.05074.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest that most non-trivial set-family operations beyond basic union, intersection, and difference inherently suffer from exponential worst-case complexity when implemented on decision diagrams.

2403.11941.problem: Constructing non-adaptive, perfect zero-knowledge probabilistically checkable proofs for high-complexity languages that remain secure against arbitrary adaptive malicious verifiers.
2403.11941.methods: The paper uses a masked sumcheck protocol over the Reed-Muller code augmented with subcube sums, employing the combinatorial nullstellensatz to enforce antisymmetric structures and introducing locally simulatable randomized encodings.
2403.11941.regime: The result applies to the complexity class #P under non-adaptive queries against arbitrary polynomial-time malicious verifiers.
2403.11941.thought_generalization: The algebraic and combinatorial techniques used to simulate subcube sums of low-degree extensions suggest that any linear randomized encoding with local characterization properties can be transformed into a perfectly zero-knowledge proof system.

2403.05418.problem: The paper characterizes and determines the computational complexity of deciding whether a regular graph admits specific vertex partitions that balance the distribution of edges.
2403.05418.methods: The authors analyze structural properties of regular graphs using independence numbers, vertex covers, and Brooks' theorem to establish equivalence conditions and prove NP-completeness via reduction.
2403.05418.regime: The results apply to finite, regular graphs, with a particular focus on cubic graphs and d-regular graphs of arbitrary order.
2403.05418.hypothesized_generalization: The equivalence between balanceability and simple balanceability in regular graphs suggests that structural constraints like regularity collapse the complexity of finding balanced edge partitions into simpler independent set problems.

2403.06694.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of finding edge-preserving mappings from input graphs of bounded diameter to odd cycles of length five or greater.
2403.06694.methods: The authors employ list-reduction techniques, neighborhood constraint analysis, and reductions to 2-SAT to design polynomial-time and subexponential-time algorithms.
2403.06694.regime: The results apply to finite, loopless, non-bipartite graphs of diameter at most 2 or 3, analyzed in the asymptotic limit of the number of vertices.
2403.06694.hypothesized_generalization: The tractability of these homomorphism problems suggests that graph homomorphism to larger odd cycles on bounded-diameter graphs may be systematically easier than standard 3-coloring.

2403.07200.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity of calculating a parameterized distance metric based on sum-like norms between structured representations of data.
2403.07200.methods: The authors construct polynomial-time reductions from NP-complete decision problems to the task of computing the p-presentation distance on combinatorial trees and algebraic persistence modules.
2403.07200.regime: The hardness results apply to all finite, finitely-presented multi-parameter persistence modules and merge trees for any parameter p in the range [1, infinity).
2403.07200.hypothesized_generalization: The proof strategy suggests that NP-hardness results for distance metrics defined by maximums can be systematically extended to metrics defined by sums or p-norms across a wide range of algebraic and combinatorial objects.

2403.06608.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity and parameterized tractability of finding balanced connected subgraphs, trees, and paths of a specified size in edge-bicolored graphs.
2403.06608.methods: The authors employ color coding, representative sets, and polynomial-time reductions to the Multilinear Monomial Detection problem, introducing a combinatorial branching-walk object called a relaxed-subgraph.
2403.06608.regime: The results apply to the theoretical setting of parameterized complexity, specifically establishing NP-completeness and designing fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms parameterized by the target subgraph size.
2403.06608.hypothesized_generalization: The introduction of the relaxed-subgraph object suggests that branching-walk formulations can be generalized to solve other constrained subgraph problems beyond Steiner trees and balanced structures.

2403.07239.problem: This paper investigates the exact computational complexity of dynamic programming algorithms on linear graph decompositions by establishing the equivalence of various parameterized problems under a unified complexity assumption.
2403.07239.methods: The authors introduce a new complexity hypothesis based on the pathwidth of the primal graph of CNF formulas and prove fine-grained equivalences using reductions between satisfiability, graph coloring, and intersection problems.
2403.07239.regime: The results apply to parameterized complexity settings, specifically analyzing algorithms parameterized by pathwidth, treewidth, and linear clique-width.
2403.07239.hypothesized_generalization: The findings suggest that fine-grained complexity barriers are governed by meta-complexity properties that cut across traditional complexity classes, unifying single-exponential, super-exponential, and XNLP-complete problems.

2403.06580.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity and algorithmic solutions for finding spanning out-trees (arborescences) and shortest path trees in edge-colored directed graphs subject to upper bounds on the number of edges of each color.
2403.06580.methods: The authors model the color-constrained subgraph problems as matroid intersection problems, utilizing graphic and partition matroids, and design direct polynomial-time algorithms for acyclic digraphs.
2403.06580.regime: The results apply to edge-colored directed graphs, specifically showing NP-hardness for general digraphs and polynomial-time solvability for directed acyclic graphs and weighted digraphs with only positive-weight cycles.
2403.06580.hypothesized_generalization: The efficient algorithms for color-constrained shortest path trees suggest that other NP-hard subgraph problems may become tractable when restricted to directed acyclic structures or when the solution space can be characterized by the intersection of at most two matroids.

2403.12213.problem: The paper addresses the problem of privately estimating the underlying generative parameters of a network from a single observed graph under node-level privacy constraints.
2403.12213.methods: The authors employ an exponential mechanism based on a sum-of-squares relaxation of a quadratic optimization problem over the polytope of doubly stochastic matrices, combined with a Lipschitz extension of the score function.
2403.12213.regime: The results apply in the asymptotic regime of large graphs for any constant number of blocks in the stochastic block model or block graphon approximation.
2403.12213.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques suggest that sum-of-squares relaxations can systematically yield computationally efficient, node-private estimators for a broader class of latent variable graph models.

2403.07524.problem: The paper investigates the decision, minimization, and maximization versions of the generalized dominating set problem, where the goal is to find a vertex subset whose intersection sizes with the neighborhoods of selected and unselected vertices belong to specified periodic residue classes modulo a given integer.
2403.07524.methods: The authors employ dynamic programming over tree decompositions, utilizing weight-vector compression and fast join operations to bound the size of the state space.
2403.07524.regime: The results apply to graphs of bounded treewidth, parameterized by the treewidth and the modulus of the residue classes.
2403.07524.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques suggest that efficient parameterized algorithms and matching Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis lower bounds can be established for other vertex-selection problems with periodic neighborhood constraints on graphs of bounded treewidth.

2403.12716.problem: Reducing the degree of the univariate polynomial product obtained when mapping multivariate polynomial multiplication into a single-variable domain to minimize subsequent computational complexity.
2403.12716.methods: Iterative Kronecker substitution, Chinese remainder theorem (CRT) reduction, and a hybrid reduction scheme operating on multivariate polynomials and their variable exponents.
2403.12716.regime: Theoretical analysis and algorithmic optimization for symbolic computation and fast polynomial arithmetic over finite fields.
2403.12716.hypotheses_generalization: Dynamic, iterative variable substitution combined with modular arithmetic can be generalized to optimize other algebraic reductions and tensor contractions where dimensionality reduction is required.

2403.12674.problem: The paper investigates the algebraic structure and embedding properties of monoids of partial and total functions, specifically comparing their finite generation, congruence simplicity, and homomorphic relationships.
2403.12674.methods: The authors construct and analyze pre-Thompson and Thompson monoids using right-ideal morphisms, prefix codes, and congruence relations to establish algebraic properties and homomorphic (non-)embeddability.
2403.12674.regime: The results apply to infinite, finitely generated monoids of functions over finite alphabets and their representation via acyclic digital circuits.
2403.12674.hypothesized_generalization: The equivalence between Thompson monoids and digital circuits hints that complex computational models can be fully characterized and classified using the algebraic structure of infinite-dimensional transformation monoids.

2403.14150.problem: The paper investigates the computational complexity and tractability of evaluating partition functions defined by symmetric tensor networks on domains of size 3 and 4.
2403.14150.methods: The authors introduce a linear recurrence relation on the tensor values, termed Fibonacci gates, and use an edge-contraction algorithm on graphs to compute the partition function in polynomial time.
2403.14150.regime: The results apply to the exact evaluation of Holant problems on connected graphs where the vertex constraints are symmetric ternary signatures satisfying specific algebraic orthogonality and recurrence conditions.
2403.14150.hypothesized_generalization: The authors conjecture that Fibonacci gates and their associated polynomial-time algorithms exist for symmetric tensor network partition functions on all higher domain sizes.

2403.13472.problem: The paper determines the minimum number of translationally-equivalent shapes required to make the problem of deciding whether they can tile the 2D plane algorithmically undecidable.
2403.13472.methods: The proof reduces Wang's domino problem to a 2D tiling problem by encoding arbitrary sets of Wang tiles into a fixed set of eight polyominoes using a meat, jaw, filler, teeth, and link construction aligned to a single coordinate grid.
2403.13472.regime: The result applies to translational tilings of the discrete 2D plane using a finite set of eight polyominoes.
2403.13472.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques suggest that the minimum number of tiles required to achieve undecidability in translational plane tilings can be reduced even further, potentially down to a single tile.

2403.14217.problem: Given a set of tasks with individual processing times, deadlines, and a hierarchical dependency structure where completed tasks contribute to a submodular objective function, the problem is to find a schedule for multiple parallel processors that maximizes the total objective value.
2403.14217.methods: The paper uses parameterized complexity analysis, dynamic programming, and fixed-parameter tractability (FPT) algorithms operating on tree-structured objective functions and scheduling constraints.
2403.14217.regime: The results apply to the exact, non-asymptotic regime of NP-hard scheduling problems, specifically when parameterized by the target objective value, the acceptable objective loss, or the total available processor-hours.
2403.14217.hypothesized_generalization: The tractability results suggest that scheduling problems with complex, tree-structured submodular objectives remain fixed-parameter tractable under deadline constraints when the target objective or the allowed deviation from the optimum is small.

2403.17766.problem: Determining the computational complexity of distinguishing between a random graph and a random graph containing a planted subgraph of arbitrary structure.
2403.17766.methods: Analyzing the performance of low-degree polynomial test statistics, specifically constant-degree subgraph counting statistics, on random graph distributions.
2403.17766.regime: The asymptotic regime where the number of vertices in the host graph grows to infinity and the degree of the polynomial test statistics remains constant.
2403.17766.hypothesized_generalization: A universal computational threshold for planted subgraph detection may exist for all subgraph structures, analogous to the Kahn-Kalai threshold for random graphs.

2403.16671.problem: The paper solves the decision problem of determining whether two elements in a group are related by an automorphism-twisted conjugacy relation, as well as the related orbit decidability problem.
2403.16671.methods: The authors construct a linear-time algorithm by mapping the algebraic structure to torus knot groups, utilizing geodesic normal forms of words, and analyzing the finite automorphism group of the presentation.
2403.16671.regime: The results apply to the class of odd dihedral Artin groups, which are one-relator, torsion-free groups defined by a two-vertex graph with an odd edge label.
2403.16671.hypothesized_generalization: The solvability of the twisted conjugacy problem and orbit decidability in this class suggests that similar algorithmic decidability results for conjugacy can be extended to broader classes of group extensions and general Artin groups.

2403.19401.problem: This paper analyzes the computational complexity and inapproximability of learning Boolean functions, specifically OR formulas and parities, when training data is only available as aggregated label proportions over small subsets of inputs.
2403.19401.methods: The authors prove NP-hardness of approximation results for learning target Boolean concepts using hypothesis classes such as constant-clause CNFs, k-DNFs, and parities, operating on collections of bags of bounded size.
2403.19401.regime: The results apply to the theoretical, worst-case computational complexity setting with constant bag sizes greater than or equal to two, under the framework of learning from label proportions (LLP).
2403.19401.hypothesized_generalization: The results suggest a fundamental computational hardness gap in learning from aggregated data when the hypothesis class is restricted to simple Boolean formulas compared to more expressive geometric representations like halfspaces.

2403.19665.problem: The paper analyzes potential logical and structural gaps in the foundational proof of syntactic incompleteness within formal axiomatic systems that represent arithmetic.
2403.19665.methods: The analysis evaluates the mapping between metamathematical predicates and primitive recursive functions, specifically examining the decidability of existential quantifiers over infinite domains of Gödel numbers.
2403.19665.regime: The analysis applies to formal, finitely axiomatized extensions of natural number arithmetic under the assumption of syntactic correctness.
2403.19665.hypothesized_generalization: The critique suggests that distinguishing between constructive verification procedures and existential assertions of provability may invalidate classical diagonal arguments used to establish undecidability.

2403.19680.problem: The paper aims to find a vertex cover of minimum size in an arbitrary undirected graph, which is a classic NP-complete combinatorial optimization problem.
2403.19680.methods: The approach uses semidefinite programming relaxations and vector representations of vertices to establish structural properties that guarantee a performance ratio strictly better than two.
2403.19680.Regime: The result applies to arbitrary, unstructured finite graphs under the assumption that semidefinite programs can be solved to arbitrary precision in polynomial time.
2403.19680.hypothesized_generalization: The techniques suggest that semidefinite programming relaxations can be systematically constrained to break the traditional approximation barriers of NP-hard graph partitioning problems.

2403.19817.problem: The paper investigates whether a restricted class of non-monotonic, adaptive selection strategies can collectively cover all elements of a target set of sequences that fail a given randomness criterion.
